In the Name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

O Granter of intellects, Possessor of favors and gifts, Creator of the heavens and the earth, Inventor of motion and time, Originator of things and place, Maker of light and darkness, Mover of the celestial spheres and orbits, adorning them with fixed stars and planets, Establisher of the earth for the various kinds of animals, minerals, and plants — Your praise endures, Your glory is exalted, Your remembrance is elevated, and Your name is sanctified. You are a King without beginning and without end. Your pre-eternity cannot be counted or enumerated, just as Your eternity cannot be measured. Preserve us with the light of Your knowledge and protect us from the turbidity of disobedience to You, by the intercession of the purest and most noble souls, especially the master of the messengers and leader of the pious, the guide of the bright-faced and radiant ones, Muhammad son of 'Abd Allah son of 'Abd al-Muttalib of the Hashimites — he who was honored with prophethood, born of the most noble of ancestors, sought after by all the prophets, the mercy sent to all the worlds, and the prophet of the believers — and upon all his companions, followers, righteous adherents, and the entire family, God's mercy be upon them all.

Thus says the most humble of servants, Zakariya ibn Muhammad ibn Mahmud al-Qazwini — may God have mercy on him — when, by divine grace, the opportunity arose to sit among the books of the learned and to be in their company, it occurred to me, as one who loves knowledge and whose best companion in all times is a book, and being moved by the verse of the Almighty: 'Do they not reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth?' — I wished to seek the truth of these wonders. If this work benefits the reader and resolves difficulties for him, then thanks be to God who grants understanding to the intelligent. Look upon the earth and reflect — even the simple-minded gain meaning from such contemplation. The purpose of this reflection and thought is to investigate the realities of things, and if one looks carefully...

One should seek the pleasures of this world and the blessings of the hereafter, and from fifty handmaidens it has been commanded that the contemplation of the created things of God the Almighty is a cause of certainty and true knowledge. Therefore the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Reflect upon the creation of God but not upon His essence.' Reflection on the judgments and decrees of the Almighty is only possible for one who knows what should be known, and thus refinement of character becomes necessary, and one finds no refuge except in the light of guidance. The poet says: this station is above the state of slumber and drowsiness of the body, and through it the health of the heart is attained.

Whoever contemplates it will find it a means to virtue; therein lies neither falsity nor error, just as a child's gaze upon stories and imaginings and the accounts of trials — the domination of secrets and injustices — purifies one of retribution and tales. It was commanded that one must not let strength and power fail; between the people of retribution, the slain and the deliverer of the slayer are discussed. Thus one comes to know this ruling, and by the grace of God the Almighty the natural science and the theoretical sciences find their place.

This meaning is that God the Almighty in His glorious Book tells the story of Khidr and Moses, and in that account Moses came and approached a certain youth, and went up a mountain. A horseman arrived and left behind a purse which he had hidden in his garment, which he then forgot, and the horseman departed. Afterward a shepherd came and found the purse and took it. Then that person arrived and, finding no trace of the horseman, struck at and killed the shepherd. The horseman returned and admitted he had forgotten, and demanded the gold coins from the sheikh, but the sheikh denied it, and Moses struck him and was about to cause his death. When Moses saw these circumstances he said: 'How is justice served in these matters?' God the Almighty then sent revelation saying: 'This sheikh had killed the horseman's father previously, and the shepherd had been in debt for exactly this amount of gold coins — therefore he was the one to repay it.' Thus God is the final Judge, and these are among His wonders.

[Marginalia: Picture / Two Horsemen / Glory be to God]

[Lower text:]
These wonders are remarkable — let it be known to the gatherings of the exalted, the just, the learned, the victorious, the glorious — Malik al-Islam — guardian of the fortress, who is adorned with the honor of rank and elevated stations of learning, generous of speech, particular and blessed in character and virtues of glory and honor — may gratitude be expressed.

May God perpetuate his blessing. He mentions some matters from previous recollections and subsequent affairs, as recorded here. Whoever looks into this book will perceive the author's purpose and understand the synthesis and compilation of those matters that are contrary to what is established. Within it, the power of the Creator over all creation is recognized, since the Sustainer who governs bodies is known, and the praise belongs to God the All-Wise, whose power the rational observer recognizes as the power of the Creator over the various wonders of creation. The different types of sensory and conceptual marvels mentioned in this book are indeed among the wonders of divine craft. The wise sayings, the useful anecdotes, the subtleties and rarities, the tales and narratives, and the special properties recorded here — all are gathered so that the reader may occupy himself with them and find in them the refinement of true knowledge. If one truly seeks to know, one must approach the subject carefully, for if at first one does not find it straightforward, this may be due to some deficiency in the conditions or some subtle point. For example, a magnet loses its power when vinegar reaches it, and can be restored by rubbing it with garlic — and similarly all things have their opposites and remedies. God Almighty is the witness that the special qualities, stories, parables, and examples gathered in this book — each arranged in its proper place — however embarrassing the effort may have been, if one reads it with attention, it will calm the soul and delight the discerning heart.

The first discourse concerns the celestial spheres, their forms, positions, and motions, presented in summary fashion. The fourth category: the sixth section, the types of ribs, and the eighth on multiplication, four times, and a thousand, the eighth: the stomach, the eighth: the kidneys, the bladder, and so on — examined and reviewed throughout.

On the Meaning of Wonder

Those senses are of one type: the first type are the outer senses, and these are five: sight, smell, taste, hearing, and touch. The first division is: attracting, repelling, retaining, and expelling. The second division concerns the faculties of the senses, and those are four: the nutritive, the preserving, the generative, and the formative. Chapter on the faculties in the service of the soul, which are five types: the common sense, imagination, estimation, memory, and fantasy. The fourth type concerns the motive faculty, and it has two kinds: the appetitive and the active. The fifth type concerns the rational faculty and its six kinds concern the practical intellect, which has four ranks: innate intelligence, acquired intelligence, active intelligence, and perfect intelligence. These concern the ranks of human observation and discernment.

As for the wonders of nations, they are divided into categories: the first is the wonders of the Arabs and their customs; the second is the wonders of the Franks (Europeans); the third is the wonders of Rome; the fourth is the wonders of the Turks; the fifth is the wonders of the Indians; the sixth is the wonders of the Ethiopians; the seventh is the wonders of the Nubians; the eighth is the wonders of the Berbers; the ninth is the wonders of the Chinese; and so on through many peoples and their crafts.

These include: the first — falconry; the second — herding; the third — medicine; the fourth — magic; the fifth — ironsmithing; the sixth — carpentry; the seventh — arithmetic; the eighth — the art of writing; the ninth — accounting; the tenth — calligraphy; and further crafts including: astrolabes, celestial calculations, talismans, incantations, perfumery, and various other arts both practical and theoretical — architecture, geometry, and the observation of beautiful forms.

The discussion is organized into: first, a mention of the essence; second, a mention of the notable properties; third, a mention of remarkable phenomena; and fourth, a mention of the animals and their wonders — the first part being about the nature of the type, and the second about mentioning the finest of that type and its properties and benefits.

The First Introduction: On the Meaning of Wonder

Wonder (ʿajab) in the divine sense is a condition that overcomes a person and prevents him from understanding the causes of things and the manner in which they produce their effects.

Wonder is a strange state that overcomes a person when a marvelous thing appears before him whose cause was not known beforehand, and whose nature cannot now be fully grasped or comprehended. When a person encounters such a thing for the first time and has not previously known its nature and origin, astonishment seizes him. One of the scholars has said: the great masters — for example, when it was related that Khān-Khānān went to the land of Zuhristān and found that in winter the snowfall becomes so severe and deep that travel becomes very difficult, and that they bury their provisions so that no dust reaches them and the air does not spoil them — and this is indeed a wonder. But if one looks at it from the perspective of true reason, everything in the world has its proper place and order, and when people observe it repeatedly over time, their astonishment gradually diminishes and it becomes familiar.

On the Meaning of Wonder

It comes to pass, and some needs are fulfilled, and the acquisition of pleasures and the removal of pains become settled—and the wonder of it is that over time these things fall away from a person. If the desire for something strange or unfamiliar counsels one with useful advice contrary to custom, the wonder fades, and one spends one's entire life without truly marveling at wonders. If you wish to test this with reason, then reflect on these exalted bodies—their grandeur, solidity, and stability. Consider the earth and sky, the vast seas with their saying "He spread out the earth" and "the sky He raised high." So then: some things are like bubbles, some like waterwheels, some quick-decaying, some long-lasting. Reflect on the motion of celestial bodies without support or pillar or attachment, and observe the stars in their paths, the differences of the east and west and the other quarters, and the four seasons with their variation of day and night. Each of these planetary bodies is balanced so that nothing is added to or taken from it. Look at the difference of colors—some red, some white, some of other hues—each moving in its own course, rising in the east and setting in the west, so that by means of the difference of day and night, the conditions for livelihood and rest are distinguished. From the height of the sky down to the depths of winter and summer, spring and autumn, all are reckoned precisely, and the scholars of verification agree that the sun traverses the circumference of the earth a hundred times in the blink of an eye. Recall what Gabriel said to the Prophet, peace be upon him, at the time of prayer, at the time of devotion: the sun passes swiftly with its sphere; reflect on the outside of the sky and the nature of sunlight and its rays, shining and glowing. Then consider the wonders of the heavens—of the stars seen and unseen—and know that what lies beyond description is vast. Look at the great pillar between earth and sky, at the stars fixed therein, and at clouds, rain, snow, hail, lightning, and thunder moving from horizon to horizon, filling the space between sky and earth. Were it to pour down all at once, the earth would be flooded and crops destroyed, yet it is measured according to need—if more than needed falls, the crops do not ripen. Thus God said: "And We send down water from the sky in due measure." Reflect on the differences of winds: some scatter seeds, some gather them, some disperse them, some bring rain—some nourish crops, some water the earth, some dry and parch—so look at the earth and how it is spread out as a carpet. Consider how, when raindrops touch the ground, countless varieties of plants and minerals are made pregnant within it. And how from it the springs and streams flow, from which people benefit all year long, and what remains over flows down to the sea. Then look at the wonders of the ocean—its enormous waves, the creatures of strange and minute form that live in it, every one of which has its counterpart on land. And the creatures of the sea—some like trees, such as coral that grows on rock underwater—and the wonders of sailing and the movement of ships upon the water, which cannot be fully described. As the saying goes: "Speak of the sea, but do not leave off"—so look at the helpers and aids found in the mountains, some of which lie buried in the earth like precious things cut from gems.

On the Classification of Created Things

When metals come into being, and some do not come to be, and when [certain things appear] like Nasr — at a given time and through a veil — then in the minerals of the earth, such as naphtha, tar, sulfur, pitch, and coal, they manifest. If one looks carefully at each stratum of earth, one then looks at the types of plants and their various forms. Look at their shapes, tastes, colors, and fragrances, and how some give nourishment to others in food; from where do they enter upon the ordered path? And for this reason, in every art there is a sign: consider the types of grains and the differences in their shapes, tastes, aromas, and benefits — wondrous things that no one can fully exhaust, nor can anyone reduce to one singular benefit. Look at the different kinds of animals: those in the air, those in the water, those on land; some walk on two legs, some on four, some on their bellies. Look at the forms of animals and the differences in their actions; so many wonders that the mind is left bewildered. Consider the crawling creatures, the animals of the desert and sea, the creatures whose nature it is to kill by their gaze and their poison — how some creatures cause intoxication by their mere scent, and the bites of many serpents cause death. Physicians and observers have noted all of these. The introduction, in two parts, on the Classification of Created Things:

Everything that exists is a created thing, and a created thing is either subsistent by itself or subsistent through another, or subsistent in essence — either distinguishable or not. If it is distinguishable, it is called Rational (ʿāqil); if it has no distinguishing faculty and is spiritual, it is called a Spirit (rūḥānī). If it is corporeal and attached to a perceiving soul, it is called a Soul (nafs); if it is corporeal but not attached to a soul, it is called a Demon (jinn); and if it has no station in itself and no station in another, it is called a Substance (jawhar). If a corporeal thing has no place it is called Abstract, while accidents of bodies are called Material Accidents, and accidents of spirits are called Spiritual Accidents — such as knowledge and power. Material accidents cannot be truly attained by themselves without a locus; if not truly attained, they exist in a place. As for weights and dimensions, they are said to be positional. If they relate to each other they are relational. If the action of one thing encompasses another thing, the five categories of error are then said to apply: either it is beneath the body, or before it, or it is purely external — its parts not [self-subsisting]; position is [then] of these categories. If the definition is not correct, even if the words are correct, the condition is not met — whether it is so or not; if it approaches [correctness] it is taken as axiomatic; if it is suspended, it is called an approximation; if it is found, it is called a demonstration — such as knowledge and ignorance. If the faculty of the heart is in doubt, sensory things include the faculty of sight — such as colors and lights — and sensory things include the faculty of hearing — such as sounds and letters — and sensory things include the faculty of smell — such as pleasant and unpleasant smells — and sensory things include the faculty of taste — such as flavors — and sensory things include the faculty of touch — such as heat and cold, moisture and dryness, heaviness and lightness, hardness and roughness and smoothness. That which exists and that which does not exist, the superior and the inferior — to distinguish between substance and matter, the sages have said: Know that God Most High created a substance, and formed from it vast numbers; the universe and much else followed from it. And it is said that God Most High divided from those two [substances] the heavens and the earth, as He has said:

'Have those who disbelieve not seen that the heavens and the earth were a joined entity, and We separated them?' (Quran 21:30)

Thus it is said: eight celestial spheres were created, and the scholars say it is so — since primordial matter must have existed, and [creation] happened thus. The manufactured things descended through the grades and ranks of the celestial domains and the earth. From men, celestial bodies, souls, forms, and other things, in this manner it is said: everything above the earth is called 'heaven,' and everything below it...

On the Wonders of the West, it Says:
9

The reading of that land is found in the words of God Most High: 'Allah, who created seven heavens and of the earth the like thereof.' That is, the first sphere is fire, the second is air, the third is water, the fourth is earth, and there are mixed spheres between these four: the first mixed between fire and air, the second mixed between fire and air, the third between water and earth—and this is called the Tabas sphere.

The destination from Egypt toward the strange West and its wonders: the influences of souls were such that the influence of corrupting forces, or the influence of celestial bodies, or whatever the scholars of Islam have established—when spirits reach the utmost purity, marvelous things and strange matters appear, by which a person's illness is healed.

Over the course of several years it came to pass that [certain] customs vanished and awe was replaced; accounts of this have been gathered. The soothsayers reported that the sages who predicted such things foretold what would befall the people of the West. It has been related from the accounts of those people who witnessed it: that the souls of those people, renowned among the inhabitants of a certain clime, gathered; and from what they possessed of special spiritual properties, it is reported by some of the sages and mystics of India that when a person sits alone in an empty place and concentrates the mind, what he seeks comes to pass.

Among the strange properties of souls it is told: a certain man was in a town, and he gathered a horse, soldiers, and people from all directions against him, and the great scholar of Tabari set out toward Isfahan. When he arrived at a gathering place, scouts and guides along the road told him: 'Depart from this people.' He considered this speech and, taking it to heart, confirmed it in his mind, turned back, and was saved.

Thus the influence of souls is real. It is related further: a sultan came [to a place] and became a Muslim, and at every victory he gained, he gave thanks. An Indian astrologer came and the sultan asked him to cast a horoscope and extract [a judgment]. The astrologer came before the sultan and the sultan described his dream: 'I saw myself aboard a ship, comfortable and at ease.' The sultan said: 'Interpret this for me.' He replied: 'You were aboard a ship at ease'—and he suggested that these words might signify peace—and having tested [the interpretation], he presented it to the sultan, who was pleased, and the matter was confirmed.

Among the wonders of the air: it is specifically reported that at times pieces [of matter] come down from the sky, reddish like copper, landing in a particular spot in the earth; and iron fragments fall from the air and, joining together, people wished to use them as iron—and from the air a kind of substance like sheets [of metal] fell, and amid lightning strikes cracks appeared in the earth, and in many places in Gilan also.

Abu al-Husayn 'Ali ibn al-Astra al-Jabri has stated that in the land of Africa, in a place resembling [a town], near a certain city, the people there heard a great noise and a mighty thunder came, and the people of the region were confounded. In the water there appeared a wondrous and pure substance, shaped like a human forearm in size; and from the earth there grew [plants], and a man would take twelve [of them] from this land, and they would provide food for the nomads; and its traces still exist in Egypt. In the land of Qazwin there is a place called Nashr, from which minerals of gold are produced abundantly, with grasses and plants in that region of Sava, and from it animals are born...

On the True Nature of the Celestial Spheres

It is remarkable that — just as one hears in such accounts — the apparitions (or wondrous visions) described: for instance, I saw examples ranging from the form of a woman from her feet to the top of her head, with the weight of a single body, having four arms and two heads and two faces, and at times playing the harp, and moving... And sometimes in a different manner, conforming with one another. And as it is recounted — such as the story of Joseph and the infant before Pharaoh, and Jesus — from these, the speech of animals becomes meaningful, as though the intermediary is the spiritual realm, or the elemental intermediary as described by Hermes, and after these, each one discovered [something], as the preface of the sages indicates with the symbol of Ram.

In the division of existents, know that every existent other than the Necessarily Existent — exalted be God — is divided into two categories. The first is the existent whose essence is not subject to alteration and change, and this became the basis for the divine word: 'And mankind was created not knowing.' The second category is every existent that constantly and permanently undergoes elaboration and detail — and as for those two, either they have a governing soul or they do not. Those without governance in this world include the Throne, the Footstool, the angels, the jinn, and the satans — as it is mentioned in the texts and traditions — and this has been established. Those that are governed include humans, who are of several kinds, and in that there is disagreement about the movements over time. And those that move along the path of transitions — such as waters, seas, minerals, animals, and what lies between heaven and earth — the winds, clouds, vapors, rains, and what comes and goes; the trees of every kind that have no end to their diversity of qualities and properties; and the forms of craftsmanship with their countless descriptions — there is not a single atom in existence that has not been perfectly crafted and placed. And in summary, the Creator said: 'There is no movement in all things save that He is ever-present in it.' And this points to His being One.

And in the realm of the higher existents, by reflection and consideration, the introduction becomes clear — on the true nature of the celestial spheres and their description. The celestial sphere is a simple body, moving in a circular manner upon a center, containing within itself the elements — neither hot nor cold, neither moist nor dry, not susceptible to separation or fusion — harder than anything else, and this book does not intend to elaborate upon that at length.

The spheres in their totality are like concentric shells, some convex and some concave, like layers of an onion. They form the known world. Some scholars divide them as follows: first the sphere of the Moon, then Mercury, then Venus, then the Sun, then Mars, then Jupiter, then Saturn, then the sphere of the fixed stars, and beyond it the Greatest Sphere (Primum Mobile). Each sphere has a body, and none of them come to rest — their motion is perpetual, and what people observe of their speeds confirms this. The sphere is compared to a perfectly measured geometric body — from the moment when the calculation began until now — such that if the Greatest Sphere completed one revolution, it would take an immense span of time.

Among these spheres, some move from east to west, like the Greatest Sphere and the Sphere of the Fixed Stars; and some move from west to east, like the other planetary spheres. Some spheres have a center coinciding with the center of the world (concentric), and some have their center outside the center of the world (eccentric); some are encompassing and some are encompassed. Each has its own description, as the details would make clear.

Some spheres carry no star upon them, such as the carrier spheres, and some carry a star (planet), such as the sphere of the orb. From this detailed account, what is called the Ptolemaic system (Talamus/Atlas) becomes clear, with the planets situated within their respective spheres. And the motions of the spheres are thus: scholars of mathematics — especially Ptolemy — have given the total count. The agreed and transmitted account is that there are two kinds of motion: the motion of the Greatest Sphere and the motion of the Sphere of the Fixed Stars, and the rest of the motions...

On the True Nature of the Celestial Spheres
11

The upper celestial spheres — each of the six [spheres above], and the Sun, and ten [degrees] from Venus, six from Mercury's sphere, and six from the sphere of the Moon — two from the sphere [of the Moon] for the orbital motion, which is gentle, and the first translational motion is in the sphere [of the Moon], which revolves around the center of the world. Each of their centers is the center of the world. The boundary of every orb is connected [to the next]; the concave surface of Mercury's sphere is joined to the [convex surface below], completing [a revolution] in a month and some days in the motion of its epicycle — moving from west to east — and governing [the lower realm]. Its orbit completes one revolution, so that it approaches the earth and then recedes. The whole [system of] spheres is divided into four spheres.

Among these, the first encompasses the earth; one of the four is the uppermost — its highest surface is tangent to the fire sphere below Mercury's sphere, and the second sphere, whose highest surface is tangent to the concave surface of Venus's sphere — and its lowest surface is the convex surface of the fire sphere, and it is called among the heavy spheres, because its plane and the plane of Venus's sphere share the same center, which is the center of the world. The third is called the eccentric sphere, because its center is outside the center of the world; it enters into the [total] sphere as a whole — its convex [surface] being tangent to the convex surface of this sphere at a shared point, and its concave [surface] being its own — indeed, they share a common layer, and that is called the perigee [apsis]. Between these two bodies, in their thickness and thinness, one of them contains the epicyclic sphere within it, the other surrounds it. The thickness of the containing sphere is more and its subtlety is less, while the contained sphere is the opposite. Each is called the moving [body].

The small spheres within the thickness of the eccentric sphere move and rotate upon it, and their center and motion constitute the [planet's] particular motion beyond the general motion of the whole sphere. This sphere has its own motion; [and] in addition to the general motion, it has a particular motion. The story told is that the thickness of the sphere — that is, from the highest level to the lowest — is 28,000 miles, and Ptolemy says that the measure of the thickness of the eccentric sphere is the measure of the sizes of the bodies of the stars within it. It should be known that this is not beyond the experts, and it is not difficult for anyone who is familiar with geometry; indeed, whoever has resolved the second proposition of Euclid's [Elements] will find these matters easy to understand.

Chapter: On the True Nature of a Star, whose place is in the lower sphere, and whose light from the sphere [of the Sun] illuminates in different shapes and colors — it is dark and has two [revolutions per] day and night — and the star [the Moon] completes [its orbit] in the two spheres. Its circuit takes approximately [one month], and each night it stays in one of the lunar mansions, of which there are twenty-eight; and when it completes one mansion and comes near the Sun, Bilal [the crescent] appears; and when [the Moon] reaches [its position], it completes [its arc] such that it is like 'the old dry date-stalk.' Thus the scholars of geometry have agreed that the body of the Moon's sphere [occupies] a quarter of a part — a hundred and ninety-two miles — and the diameter of the body of the Moon's sphere is approximately forty-four miles. This is what the geometers have agreed upon.

Chapter: On the Cause of the Phases of Moonlight — How the Moon receives and reflects light: it is evident to anyone that whoever faces [the Sun] is illuminated. When the Moon is in conjunction with the Sun, the illuminated half faces the Sun; and as the Moon moves away [from the Sun] into the eastern sky, the dark half faces westward, gradually receiving more light until it becomes a crescent. The farther it moves from the Sun, the more of its body receives [light]; when it is fully opposite the Sun, the side facing the Earth is fully illuminated, and people call it the full moon [badr]. Then, as it approaches the Sun again, its light diminishes and its body shrinks until it is once more in conjunction with the Sun.

Chapter: On the Cause of Lunar Eclipses — When the body of the Earth intervenes between the body of the Moon and the body of the Sun, a lunar eclipse occurs.

On the Reality of the Celestial Spheres

The node [of the Moon] has been established, and [the Moon] was approaching opposition, and the body [of the Moon] was in a position before the Earth such that the Earth's cone [of shadow] extended—the base of which is the middle of the Earth—from the rays of the Sun; and the midpoint of the Earth's shadow reaching [the Moon], its sides tapering, not reaching the full shadow cone. If one considers the latitude [of the Moon] from the ecliptic, and the Moon's disk comes into the shadow cone of the Earth's disk and passes through the center of the shadow, then the eclipse becomes total. If, however, [the Moon's latitude] is somewhat more than the Earth's disk [shadow], only part of it will be obscured.

[Section:] On the special properties of the Moon — It has been said that its influences are through moisture, since [the Moon] is temperate in heat. When [the Moon] is in the south or moving toward the west, moisture increases and clouds gather and rain spreads across the regions and night winds arise. And wherever this westward position falls, that is the peak of moisture. And every day [the Moon] rises and the tides increase, and they recede, and the waters and great waves arise from the depths below, and a mighty wind comes from high above, and the sea becomes rough and turbulent and waves mount; and when [the Moon] is in the zenith and the tides recede, calm prevails on the sea and sailors can reach port, and if they are at sea they face great danger. And the wood [cut during a full Moon] will be wide and deep and of good quality, and trees will flourish. And when [the Moon] is in a favorable position, the orchards and forests will flourish and their places will be full of plants, and benefit will arise from them.

And whenever all these conditions are combined — that is, when the [Moon's] light is full on every day of increase, and [remains] in increase until the time of opposition, then begins to wane — at the time of conjunction and opposition, winds arise, and at these times the Moon's influences on animals make their moisture increase, and the humor and nourishment grow more and the body's temperament and natural heat improve. And after the crisis [of an illness], the animal grows weak and the fine channels contract and the dominant temperament wanes. Physicians say that the conditions of the humors and what befalls them depend on the increase and decrease of the Moon.

Some say: whoever begins something on the day of the new Moon and with its [initial] light will complete it swiftly and it will come easily and powerfully; but if [the Moon] is waning, the opposite holds, and the milk of animals is more plentiful when the Moon is full and bright, and if it is deficient in light the opposite is the case, and the first nights' milk is more. And some say: if these things proceed — that is, when the Moon is above the horizon in the eastern quarter its light is full, and in the western quarter it acts as though lacking in light, and when below the horizon the opposite of this applies — then if one studies these matters, the Moon's influences become clear.

And among the Moon's influences: if someone wears clothing left in the moonlight, headache and cold will afflict them and their temperament will be disturbed; and if animals eat food that has been left under the moonlight, it becomes spoiled. Fish from the sea whose flesh has been corrupted are more harmful in the first half [of the lunar month]; and the movement of reptiles, insects, and stinging creatures is more [frequent] in the first half [of the lunar month].

And among the Moon's influences: when trees are cut while the Moon is full and bright, they yield more timber and their wood is heavier and more durable; but if cut while the Moon is waning, they fall faster and their timber is lighter, and their fruits, grains, and produce are also affected likewise. And in this way, growth is greatest at the [Moon's] beginning [of increase], and [the Moon] provides moisture and nourishment throughout, and its manifest and hidden effects on nature are [as described].

On the Description of the Celestial Spheres

When [the moon] is at half-disc, the reflection of its face shows a wonderful hue, and its color varies in a strange manner. The influence of its conjunction with [other planets] causes its appearance to change dramatically, and the rays that emanate from it differ according to its relation to the fixed stars. Half of it faces toward the sun and half away, giving various colors from yellowish to white. Through the influence of these conjunctions the pure essences of gems become activated, and the medical properties of substances are augmented or diminished. When combined with Saturn, its yellow hues appear; it has the power to dry excessive moisture, and by nature cures black bile, which is greatly beneficial.

First Section: Know that astronomers hold different views on this matter, and the philosophers have truly verified that in certain copies it is stated that some stars in close proximity to one another — which the Arabs call Umm al-Hawm — are said to be of beneficial influence when together, while others consider them harmful to certain people. During the first part of the night they are seen in the northern or southern parts of the sky, but for most of the night they move from east to west, and the sphere revolves continuously.

Second Section: On the sphere of Mercury — its upper surface is connected to the sphere of Venus, and its lower surface to the sphere of the Moon. It revolves completely from west to east once in a full year, since its eccentric sphere and its epicycle both move outside the center, and this is why astronomers call it doubly eccentric. Mercury moves swiftly in both its sphere and its epicycle; in this way the sphere of Mercury has an upper surface and a lower surface, totaling forty-two thousand and something degrees altogether. 

As for the properties of Mercury: the astrologers call Mercury of neutral influence — if it is with a benefic planet, it becomes benefic, and if with a malefic, it becomes malefic. When it is well-situated, it bestows intelligence, understanding, and sharpness of mind, and this intelligence is used toward good ends; but when poorly situated, it directs these same faculties toward deception and trickery. In any matter over which it presides, when Mercury is close to the sun it becomes invisible, and as stated, it can govern bodily constitution, lands, spherical geometry, nobility, and greatness. 

Third Section: On the sphere of Venus — its upper surface is connected to the sphere of the Sun, and its lower surface to the sphere of Mercury. It completes its revolution from west to east in one year. The sphere of the Sun is like Venus: every three days, when Venus moves swiftly, it advances ahead of the Sun; the full account of this can be found in the section on retrograde motion. The thickness of the sphere of Venus — that is, the distance between its upper and lower surfaces — is nine thousand, nine hundred and forty-five miles.

Section on the Properties of Venus: Venus is called the Lesser Benefic, because its hours are close to those of Jupiter. In every house it presides over, it brings warmth, delight, music, and adornment. It is said that its aspect creates affection between people, and that when a lover gazes upon someone under Venus's influence, love takes firm hold and grows between them. It is also said that if Venus is well-configured at the time of a marriage, both men and women will enjoy wonderful prosperity. The body of Venus — that is, its diameter — is thirty-eight parts of the Earth's diameter, and the diameter of its body is one hundred and forty-something miles.

Fourth Section: On the sphere of the Sun — its upper surface is connected to the highest sphere, and its lower surface borders the sphere of Venus...

On the Properties of Stars and Animals

Mars reigns over its sphere and travels from west to east in a complete year; it is considered the ruler of the earth and stands outside the center of the celestial system, as has been described in the discussion of the celestial spheres. Its grace surpasses that of others in the orbit of the sun, since the sun's sphere of influence is bound up with its proximity and distance to other bodies. If the sun were always in its position, it would bring winter or summer in turn, and its light would be constant; the people and plants would flourish under its warmth. But if it continued in this way, the excessive heat of summer would destroy everything through its burning, and similarly, if the cold became too great, all things would perish from the cold. Therefore the ecliptic has been arranged with 360 degrees and many parts, dividing the year into seasons—and this is an excellent arrangement.

It is known that the sun is positioned in the fourth sphere, and from this position it maintains a balance among the heavenly bodies. If it were in the first sphere, everything would burn from excessive heat, and its subtlety and grace would be lost. Furthermore, if the sun were fixed in one position of great heat or great cold, it would not be able to sustain life. But as it moves each day through a different region, moving through its arc, it maintains balance. The diameter of the sun's sphere is said to be 166 times that of the earth, and by traveling a certain portion of degrees each day, it causes changes among the other planets.

The properties of the sun that have been mentioned are among its great benefits, and of its influences it is said: when it enters the degree of its position and the atmosphere changes because the cold of the air is different—so the atmosphere changes and it produces rain and the earth becomes fertile and rivers and streams flow from it—and so plants and animals come to life. It is He who sends the winds as glad tidings, and these are the signs of His mercy. Its effects on minerals are that it purifies the earths and coagulates the waters, so that minerals are generated and developed in the ground, such as gold, silver, copper, iron, lead, and others. The properties of each metal are well known, as are those of plants and vegetation.

In places where the sun does not reach, its beneficial rays do not arrive—in such dark depths the sun's warmth does not penetrate. It is such that when the sun rises to its midpoint, all things stand in balance and equilibrium. When the sun reaches its zenith it begins its decline, and the plants begin to wither and droop; and when the sun sets, they wilt further. Another day comes with its dew refreshing them. As for animals, when the morning light appears, the animals begin to move and show vitality until noon; then as the sun declines, their energy gradually decreases until sunset, when the animals retire to their lairs and the working animals rest.

It is remarkable that they say: the people over whom the sun shines most brightly—like the people of Sudan and the Arabs—their bodies are dark and their constitution is weak, and their dispositions are like those of a colocynth in pungency. But those over whom the sun is more moderate—their color is fair, their faces broad and noble, their light radiant and their complexion white.

On the Nature of the Stars and Their Properties

This section discusses the celestial spheres and their movements. According to ancient authorities, the outermost sphere completes one revolution every thirty-six thousand years. When the northern regions are in disorder, the southern become well-ordered, and vice versa, such that one quarter lies under water, another is dry land, the third faces north in ruin and the fourth prospers — this is how the seasons arise, for the great sphere interposed between the sun and the observers acts as a veil, so that the observers are shaded and the rays are cut off.

For this reason, when the ecliptic is positioned along the houses of the zodiac at ninety degrees, the sun passes through the zodiacal belt and shifts. Part of it turns northward and another part drifts, so that certain declinations are fixed while others move. The distances and diameters mentioned by Ptolemy for the sphere of Mars are given: the radius of the epicycle of Mars is described as the smallest in the sequence, because its nature is one of harshness, subjugation, harm, destruction of wealth, and distress. The diameter of the sphere of Mars is one thousand and fifty-eight miles.

As for the sphere of Jupiter: it is described as auspicious — its properties bring good fortune, joy, and blessings. The diameter of Jupiter's sphere is given along with its period. According to Ptolemy, Jupiter's great orb measures one thousand three hundred and some hundreds of miles in diameter. Jupiter completes its circuit from west to east in twelve years and some days.

As for the sphere of Saturn: it is said to bring ruin, disaster, sorrow, grief, and long suffering. Its sphere completes one revolution in approximately twenty-nine and a half years. The diameter of Saturn's orb is given in the same manner.

The section then turns to the retrograde motion and stations of the planets (Retrogradation and Stationing of the Planets): when a planet is carried on its epicycle and the motion of the epicycle runs contrary to the motion of the deferent sphere, the planet appears to move backward (retrograde); when the two motions are equal, it appears stationary; when they run in the same direction, it moves swiftly forward (direct). The sphere of the fixed stars is above the sphere of Saturn; its upper boundary adjoins the greatest sphere and its lower boundary adjoins the sphere of Saturn. It moves from west to east, and it carries the multitude of the fixed stars.

On the Nature of the Stars and Their Properties

In the hundred years that a zodiacal sign traverses, which amounts to thirty-four complete years, Ptolemy established correctly that the swift and noble stars of this sphere are arranged thus — and through approximate reckoning the diameter of the sphere of the swift stars, their intellect and essence, and from measuring their diameter Ptolemy worked it out — those who follow this reckoning know how the lines and diameters are drawn. Since it is not possible to measure the spheres and stars without geometry, for to every difficult matter there is a path, and whoever has studied the fundamentals of measurement has made it easy to understand, and from its assemblage of the ethereal bodies in combinations — [here follows a chapter heading] Chapter on the Third Stars and Their Good Influences — the sages have said the total of seventeen stars, and from these eight stars result, so Ptolemy brought forth and some books say some of these are in northern degrees and some on the ecliptic, and every star is either of good degree or otherwise. They are named according to human forms — some in the shape of people, some in the shape of animals, like Cancer; some in the shape of birds, like Aquila; some in the shape of other animals, like Libra and Scorpio; some in the shape of river creatures; and some are half-figure, half-animal, like Centaurus. And so it is that when a complete form becomes like another, the star of one figure is in relation to another — this means that if any star is located there, it is known, and the number twelve hundred and two stars and one hundred [are counted]. When the forms are compiled together, they are called 'the images of the stars.' The star at the head of Aries is what the astronomers call the 'surveyor,' and from that figure of the ram it is eight degrees in the north and twelve on the ecliptic and twelve to the south, and the chapter on the northern figures: those figures are three hundred and sixty-two stars total, and the small bear — Ursa Minor — is close to the north pole, and its stars are recorded; seven stars make up its figure and three others are outside it arranged in a square. The four that form the tail are called Banat al-Na'sh [daughters of the bier], and those on the edge of the tail are called the boundary stars, known as the 'equatorial boundary.' The star Kaukabat al-Dubb al-Asghar [the star of the Little Bear]: its stars are nine in the figure and outside the figure are the terrifying ones, and its image is known as 'the bright ones,' and three that are on the tail are called the ancients — those in the middle are of that type. CHAPTER ON THE LUNAR MANSIONS

The lunar mansions are twenty-eight in number. Approximately, every fourteen mansions are above the horizon and fourteen are below; whenever one [set] rises, the other sets, and from dawn onward, [the moon] traverses them again. The scholars say that [the moon] has a circuit through the seven planets, and by these mansions the Arabs determined the times of rain, dew, heat, cold, and events of the year — the year of plenty or scarcity — and from these mansions they derived judgment about conditions. These mansions are divided into two parts: the first group is called the Syrian [northern] mansions, beginning with al-Sharatayn, and the last of the first [group] is al-'Aqrab; the second group they call the Yamani [southern] mansions, beginning with al-'Aqrab and ending with al-Risha'. [The first mansion] al-Sharatayn consists of two stars; the distance between them in appearance is about thirty [degrees], and when they reach the middle of the sky, their elevation above the southern stars increases, and when the sun enters [this mansion], night and day become equal, the new year begins, spring arrives, Sharatayn returns to conjunction, and [the season] becomes complete.

Al-Butayn: they describe it thus — al-Butayn means the belly, and it consists of three small dim stars between al-Sharatayn and the Pleiades. When al-Butayn sets, movement comes [in weather], winds pass through, and insects emerge from underground — ants and small creatures appear beneath the earth. Some say: if rain falls during this mansion, the year will be one of scarcity; and some say: if a person looks upon it, [they say] 'May God bless your travel.' The first produce of the earth and milk increase, and the first of produce, milk, sedge, and colocynth [appear]. Al-Butayn is close to the Pleiades.

On the Description of the Stars and Their Conditions

The text reads that [the compiler] has described two stars called Akhir Fara' and Na-Mu'akhkhar, and Na-Fara', which are the first parts of the third section. It is mentioned that these resemble plums and quinces. If cold weather prevails during this period, it brings rain and various fruits. Al-Farj has been mentioned in the first section. There is abundant rainfall and it becomes cold. The nights and days become equal in length. The belly of the Milky Way contains stars arranged in the form of rings, and a tail on one side and a head on another side. In the first rank no star is absent, and in the second rank stars fill the middle of the row, and when these appear, fine weather comes and much rain follows, bringing good fruits such as pebbles and grapes.

Each season has seven turns of observation, and each turn is nineteen days long, and one day is added to each so that the year reaches three hundred and sixty-five days. This is the measure by which the sun traverses the entire sphere, and it has been said that its rising is like a fixed point in the east and its setting in the west. The sphere of the Zodiac and the sphere of fixed stars are like other celestial spheres. That imaginary circle is such that when the sun travels from east to west and completes its course, from the center of the sun an imaginary circle is conceived: if that circle cuts through the world, the supreme sphere is cut by it, and the resulting imaginary circle is called the ecliptic, for it is conceived as the center of the world. This circle cuts the equator at two opposite points. The two poles of the world produce the north and south celestial poles, and the equator is cut [by the ecliptic]. The point of intersection on the sphere of the zodiac and the equator, known as the autumnal equinox, is on one side. Circles are conceived from the poles of the equator within the sphere. The ecliptic divides the sphere into four equal parts: the first quarter, Spring, is from the vernal equinox to the summer solstice, and that period is the season of spring; the second quarter is from the summer solstice to the autumnal equinox, and that duration is the summer season; the third quarter is from the autumnal equinox to the winter solstice, and that period is autumn; the fourth quarter is from the winter solstice back to the vernal equinox, and that duration is winter.

From the poles of the ecliptic [great circles] go out, and from the pole of the ecliptic for the summer and spring quarters, we conceive circles — each passing through the pole of the ecliptic — that divide the sphere. Since these circles go outward from the poles of the ecliptic and the world is divided into twelve parts, each twelfth part is called a sign (burj). Thus the sphere of the fixed stars is divided into twelve signs as described, and the stars in each sign take different forms — some in the shape of a knot, others triangular — as their names indicate.

Among the special qualities of the Angel of Death: "O Angel of Death, I greet you greatly," he replied: "By the One Who created me rightly, I would represent you between two moments, carrying you away in six steps." He goes from the heavens, having traveled a thousand years, going as far as the eye can see, with the likeness of God. His body has filled everything — what is between East and West has been traversed by him. If God willed, you and everything that is between heaven and earth — he could see it all. Solomon said: "Have you come to visit, or to take the soul?" He said: "To visit you, for every day I pass by your house to visit Solomon." Solomon asked: "How are people?" He replied: "From Babylon I bring knowledge and the names of the people of the months. In another year, for the people of monotheism, I take their souls from the right hand, and for the polytheists from the left hand. I convey them from a place filled with pitch, and it is as if..." When the Angel of Death came to visit Solomon again, one of those present looked and then left without being noticed. Solomon said: "That was death that passed over and left." The Angel of Death said: "That was death — I was there in that place, but it was only a matter of God's decree regarding that man." He then instructed him, and he was brought. The Angel of Death came to Solomon again to visit, and Solomon asked: "What happened — that man looked without being noticed by you?" The Angel of Death said: "I was commanded, and the decree of death for the people of India was near, and I was to take his soul very soon, and I was to take him there."

On the Ranks of the Angels of the Heavens:
It is difficult to recount, but it is said that the angels of the heavens are constantly in glorification (tasbih), in praise (tahlil), in standing (qiyam), in supplication (qunut), in bowing (ruku'), in prostration (sujud), and again in standing — in worship of God, night and day without ceasing, until the Day of Resurrection. It is said that the angels of heaven and earth have the form... and the chief of the angels of the first heaven has the form of him, and his name is Isma'il. In the second heaven they are depicted in images, and the chief of those angels is known by a certain name.

On the Story of the Angels and [Harut and Marut]

Some say that four [guardian angels] are present during the day and two at night, and that even unbelievers have a guardian [angel], because the mention of guardianship is stated in general terms, as where it is said "surely there are watchers over you" and "noble recorders."

When a servant commits a sin, the companion on the left should hold back from recording it for a longer moment — if the person repents of that sin, it should not be written down. In another narration it is said: when the right-hand companion speaks to the left-hand companion and says, "What is the state [of this person]?" he replies, "He did such-and-such." It is narrated from the Prophet (peace and blessings of God be upon him and his family) that for every servant two angels are appointed as keepers, to record all deeds. When one passes away, the spirit of so-and-so departs, and the angel says, "God forgive him," and the people of the earth say the same, and the people of heaven say the same. The merit of this is recorded in paradise. 

It is narrated in this manner from the Messenger of God that when the angels spoke before God about the sons of Adam and what they did, and said, "We would not do as they do," the Prophet said: "If you were in their situation, you would sin as they do." Thus two angels were sent down — Harut and Marut — and a woman named Zahra [Venus] was sent to tempt them. The two angels sinned through her and their purity was gone. Then they were given a choice [between punishment in this world or the next], and they chose punishment in this world. They are now suspended between heaven and earth as a torment until the Day of Resurrection.
