[Illustration caption on right margin, lower]: Image of Harut and Marut

On the Page of the Angels and Their Request

In the Afterlife he looked at it and said: 'What is it to me?' And he replied: 'The punishment of this world is finite, but the punishment of the afterlife is not.' So he chose the punishment of this world, and it descended upon him.

It has come from this image that Harut and Marut are both suspended upside-down in chains in a place upon the earth of Babylon until the Day of Resurrection. And in another narration it is said that the Most High said to them...

HARUT                    HARUT

[Description of the illustration: Two figures hanging upside down between trees]

He sent them down and said that the greatest sins to avoid are sorcery, murder, theft, and fornication. He informed them that in a single day all four of these transgressions were committed by them. In the time of Aristotle it is said that women's measure of [virtue]... The angels passed over the men through days and nights, which are then divided into centuries, decades, years, months, days, hours, and the hours of days and nights are for human beings. Each person in this transient world has a livelihood and every hour has the capacity for that person to attain felicity through it.

The result is that the perfection of human souls lies in their contentment, and as the wise one has said in verse: 'Sovereignty exists in the realm of lessons; its pleasure is found among those who seek wisdom.' Like a growing plant that is cut off from its roots annually, and every week is visited [by the gardener], and every moment is tended — inevitably the distance must be covered, with the belief that Providence and the movements of the celestial spheres are its causes.

And the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Do not curse time, for God is time.' A day in religious law is from the rising of dawn until the setting of the sun, and the night is from the setting of the sun until its rising. Day and night together are twenty-four hours. The longest day occurs at the summer solstice — approximately fifteen hours of day and nine of night. Then the days shorten and the nights lengthen, until the eighteenth [of the relevant month] when day and night are equal. Then the night continues to grow until the seventeenth of the first Kanun [December], which is the longest night — fifteen hours — and the day is nine hours. After that the days begin to lengthen and the nights to shorten, until the twentieth of Adar [March] when day and night are again equal — each twelve hours. As the Almighty, the All-Knowing has ordained: God alternates night and day. Know that the Lord has created the sea from which cold comes; and from it, through God's grace, sleep overtakes one at the appointed time, and God through His grace and kindness at a fixed time stirs the sea, which is its remedy, and then...

On the topic of the Imam and the special properties of days

It has been established for the purpose of tranquility — that night is for rest so that at the time of movement everyone is still, and at the time of stillness everyone is at rest — otherwise, if people seek something and the affairs of men come to a halt, from this comes the corruption of the land. As God said: 'We made the night and the day for you, so that you might rest in it and seek of His bounty.' A chapter on the merits of the days and the special properties of Friday: Friday is the festival of the people of Islam and the master of the days. In this manner it is narrated that the noble prophets declared that the best day that rises is Friday. On this day God Almighty accepted repentance, and on this day He created [Adam], and on this day He increased His bounty, and on this day He accepts repentance. He who is engaged in [devotion] on this day, God will grant him His grace, for it is the door of the Most Gracious. Whoever seeks from God on the night of Friday and the day of Friday, God will grant his request from His great bounty. And it is said that whoever on Friday reveals his illness, it will leave him and he will be healed. It is said: 'Friday is the best of days, and the gathering on Friday is a day of festival.'

Friday is the festival of Moses — so it is said — and it has been reported that the Prophet said: 'Every page [of deeds] is presented, and every matter comes to rest.' They say that on Friday God Almighty finished [the work of] creation. It is said that whoever is occupied on Friday, the trees and all things bear witness against him. Among the people of Islam it should not be contradicted, as has been said: 'Be gentle with your companion on Saturday' — meaning that those who observe Saturday, if they carry [goods] on Friday, the following year it will bear no fruit. The Christians call it the first day, for it is the first of the days of the world. Jesus commanded his people to celebrate Friday as a feast, saying: 'After your feast I have a feast for you.' The first day — Sunday — was chosen, and every one who begins on Sunday, until Monday it will be blessed.

Monday is the most blessed of days. The Prophet, peace be upon him and his family, was asked about fasting on Monday. He replied: 'On this day deeds are raised up, and sorrows are lifted, and on this day Ahmad ibn Hanbal narrates that the Prophet was born, and on this day revelation descended, and on this day he arrived in Medina, and on this day he passed away.'

Tuesday is a day of war and bloodshed, and one should occupy oneself with self-improvement and refinement and the like. It is said that whoever travels on Tuesday, he will return.

Wednesday — on this day Pharaoh and his host drowned. Some call it the day of ill fortune. Ali, peace be upon him, said: 'The last Wednesday of the month is a day of continuous ill fortune.' After this, the sight of the afflicted people improved.

Thursday is a day recommended for fulfilling needs, beginning journeys, and writing letters. Ibn Malik narrates that the Prophet, peace be upon him and his family, was asked about the days. He replied: 'Friday is a day of generosity; the Quraysh performed certain acts on this day. Saturday is a day of commerce and deception. God Almighty began [His creation] on Sunday. Monday is a day of travel and commerce. Tuesday is a day of hardship and blood was shed [on it]. Wednesday Pharaoh was drowned, and God destroyed him. Thursday is the day for fulfilling needs.' He praised Abraham and honored the sun and fulfilled [needs] on this day.

On the Description of Days and Events

Ali ibn Abi Talib — the Lion of God, the Conqueror, the Commander of the Faithful, the Prince of the Believers, and the Vanquisher of the Wicked — recorded certain auspicious and inauspicious days of the week. He said: Sunday is a day of planting and cultivation; Monday contains such-and-such qualities in creation; Tuesday carries its own qualities; Wednesday brings certain remedies; Thursday is a day for fulfilling wishes and needs, for it is the day of men's pleasures alongside women; Friday is the day of assembly (gathering) and of the various classes of people. We shall, in this book, relate the customs and traditions of the Arabs, Persians, and Romans, and mention some of the regions.

Section on the Months of the Arabs: The months are reckoned from new moon to new moon, and the year is agreed to consist of twelve months — two of which complete the lunar cycle — so that each month is divided accordingly. As God Most High says: 'The number of months with God is twelve months in God's Book.' We shall now mention some of the qualities of each month.

Muharram is a month of blessing; its name means 'sacred/forbidden,' signifying that obedience in it brings increased reward, and sins committed in it bring greater punishment. The First of Muharram is the festival of the Arabs, just as Nowruz is the festival of the Persians, and some call it the Day of Celebration. Many auspicious events took place in it. The Day of Ashura (the tenth) is also well-known: on that day Adam's repentance was accepted; Noah's ark came to rest on Mount Judi; Abraham was born; Jesus was born; the fire became cool for Abraham; Jacob's sorrow was relieved; Joseph was freed from the well; Solomon was restored to his kingdom; David's repentance was accepted; the trial of Jonah's people was lifted; the affliction of Job was removed. There are many other events recorded for this day. However, it is also the day on which Imam Husayn was martyred, and afterward it became a day of mourning. The Shia mark this day with grief, and using kohl (antimony) on this day is said to be beneficial for eyesight. Those who oppose this practice are condemned. The sixteenth marks the coming of the Army of the Elephant (Abraha's army), when the people of Saffron Elephant arrived; some say this was inauspicious.

Safar: It is said that this month is also one in which caution is advised, since some people consider it unlucky and refrain from travel and important undertakings. However, the Prophet is reported to have said that whoever travels in Safar will be protected and return safely. The first of Rabi' al-Awwal: the gates of goodness and happiness are opened for the world, for the Prophet (peace be upon him) was born on its twelfth day, and on its eighteenth day he arrived in Medina. The last ten days of Rabi' al-Awwal are also mentioned.

Jumada al-Awwal: On the eighteenth day, the army of Hajjaj ibn Yusuf entered and besieged the fortification of Ubayd Allah ibn Zubayr. On its twenty-second day, the Commander of the Faithful (Ali) met certain events. The Shia consider some days of this month blessed.

Jumada al-Akhira: On one of its days, Ibn Zubayr rebuilt with his own hands, based on a tradition he received from others. It is also mentioned that certain people transferred their allegiance from one group to another, whether willingly or unwillingly, at this time.

On the Days and Their Special Properties

Ibrahim [ibn al-Zubayr] had built that structure [the Ka'ba]; when al-Hajjaj demolished it, the present structure that exists today is his [al-Hajjaj's] work. Rajab is a blessed month; it is called Shahru'llah (the Month of God), and also 'al-Asabb' meaning it pours forth [mercy], and 'al-Asamm' meaning peaceful. Reward and forgiveness descend upon servants in this month, and many nights and days pass in which worship is accepted and prayers are answered. If someone wishes to make a supplication and have it granted, let him do so in this month. I [the author] came across in history that Ibn Jas came near the Amir and sat, and I was also near him. The Amir said: 'I have not seen anyone who looks to me more [knowledgeable].' [The man] said: 'Among the best of the devout is al-Sal'i, who fasts in Rajab and makes supplications.' The Amir said: 'Bring him to me.' When he came, the Amir said: 'Recite to me your Jahiliyya poetry.' He said: 'O Amir, [the affairs of] the Jahiliyya have passed, and Islam has come, and the affairs of Jahiliyya are now void.' The Amir said: 'The best of Jahiliyya poetry — tell it.' He said: 'O Amir, in the time of ignorance I was wronged; many oppressed me and I had no recourse to God and no patience.' Then Rajab came and I made supplication, saying: 'I call upon none but You, O God, for You alone suffice.' Then the man rose and departed. The Amir said: 'Glory be to God! How wonderful!' — and from that time there was relief.

The fifteenth night [of Sha'ban] is called the Night of Intercession; the seventh is the Night of the Ascension (Mi'raj); and Sha'ban is also a blessed month. It is said that in this month fates and provisions are arranged and mercy descends. A narration states: 'On this night God Almighty looks upon His creation and forgives all except the polytheist and the one who harbors enmity.' God Almighty on the fifteenth night of Sha'ban forgives as many souls as the number of hairs on the sheep of [the tribe of] Kalb. In that time, no one spends [this night in worship] more than the shepherds of Kalb.

In this month one should devote oneself [to worship]. The ancient [scholars] observed that Bayt al-Maqdis and Bayt al-Haram are the most noble. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: 'Sha'ban is the month of God, Sha'ban is my month, and Ramadan is the month of my community.' Abu Dharr al-Ghifari narrates that in this night one rises and draws near [to God], and it is the eighth [night], called the Night of Protection — some say [Laylat al-Qadr] is the twenty-fifth, and some say the twenty-seventh. The Abbasids rose to power in Khurasan in the year [related to] Abu Shir. Some say Laylat al-Qadr is the twenty-seventh; according to some narrations, on that night angels descend to assist Muslims. The first [of these blessed days]: on this day God Almighty accepts the repentance of the repentant, and on this day Gabriel (Jibril) was chosen for revelation; and on this day the Prophet traveled to [the heavens] and his companions [followed]; and on this day Maryam and the Helpers [Ansar] were blessed.

In these days life's accounts are drawn up. Dhu'l-Qa'da is also one of the sacred months (al-ashhur al-hurum), and among its blessings: the Arabs and non-Arabs would refrain [from fighting] in it. On its eighth [day], God Almighty gave to Moses (peace be upon him) the two tablets [of the Law]. On the day of the Companions [of the Cave?], it is said that Abraham and Ishmael raised the foundations of the Ka'ba. On the twelfth of this month...

On the Description of the Imam and the Seasons

In the name of God. The sea split for him, and on the twenty-second of Jonah (Yunus), fish came out of the water, and on this day the yaqtin tree (gourd) grew its leaves abundantly so that it provided shade, and the twenty-second of Dhu'l-Hijja is called that because of it. The sacred days of pilgrimage — the "well-known days" — are called the four days of it; this day is called Yawm al-Tarwiyya because at the watering places in Islam, at the shadow of the Masjid al-Haram, the pilgrims water themselves. The day of Arafat is called so because the pilgrims gather at the plain of Arafat and recognize one another. This is also the day of Eid al-Ghadir, and on this day blessings and peace upon the Commander of the Faithful were sealed, and the covenant of brotherhood was made. On this day forgiveness descended, and the seal of the knowledge of the first, the most famous month, came — the act on this day was as follows: counting from the first year of the Hijri calendar: the first is Muharram, the second Safar, the third Rabi' al-Awwal, the fourth Rabi' al-Akhir, the fifth Jumada al-Ula, the sixth Jumada al-Akhira, the seventh Rajab, the eighth Sha'ban, the ninth Ramadan, the tenth Shawwal, the eleventh Dhu'l-Qa'da, the twelfth Dhu'l-Hijja — twenty-nine or thirty days each, as you know. The first day of any month should be the day that the new moon is seen. It is reported from Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq that he said: if the first of Ramadan is unclear for someone, let them take the day that was the last day of last year's Ramadan and count forward — that will be the first of next year's Ramadan. This calculation has been used as a reliable method up to the present.

The months of the Romans (Byzantines/Syrians) differ, as their months correspond to the movement of the sun, and the sun's movement differs in each season — some days are longer, some shorter — as the tradition narrates. Therefore some of their months are thirty days, some thirty-one, some twenty-eight, so that altogether they come to three hundred and sixty-five days. The names of the Roman months are: Tishrin al-Awwal, Tishrin al-Akhir, Kanun al-Awwal, Kanun al-Akhir, Shubat, Adhar, Nisan, Iyar, Haziran, Tammuz, Ab, Aylul — and Tishrin and Kanun are the earliest and latest.

When Tishrin al-Awwal begins, the waters become good and the springs are strengthened; winds come from the south; the sea is agitated and storms arise; armies move and raids occur; if rain falls it is good, and if it is dry it is harmful to people.

Kanun al-Akhir: southerly winds come, springs freeze, olives and olive oil are preserved; rain falls, the land is moistened, the sea off Persia is stormy; if at the start of this month there is disturbance at sea off Persia, the waves will be great and the vegetation will harden.

Kanun al-Awwal: on the first day, trading is good and energetic, and commanders make expeditions; physicians advise against eating beef on this day; do not drink cold water or sleep in the open; after the middle of this month, the streams begin to dry up and decline, the waters recede, the night lengthens, and the birds begin to gather.

On the Letter B (Ba)

The Nile increases and there is rain; the leaves of trees fall. After drinking [the water] well, those who speak say that when such-and-such falls in the water, whoever drinks from the spout will become satisfied. This is one of the reasons for the refreshment of the common people. The cause of the cooling of the air is that if cold water is drawn from the spout, it is said that the honored Ezra (Uzayr) sat by the shore and established the 'Red Hearth' (Kanun al-Ahmar). This marks the beginning of the season, and the appearance of the Christians is at the time of the killing of those who steer by it. When a certain hour comes, the bees swarm forth; the master of Laodicea (Latakia) departs from it, and the birds begin to arrange their nests, and along with the birds, partridges and swallows come, and the swift (khattaf) arrives. The warm winds blow upward and the creatures come out from inside the earth, as they emerge upward. The birds call and flutter.

The 'fall of the third phase' is what the Arabs call in their language 'the intensification of winter.' They built three houses to shelter from it, warming themselves with fire in the first house, and the second house was in the middle level, and the third house was in the lower level. The camel and the livestock were in the first house, and the people were in the third house. It was as cold as a bitter winter. In the first phase, when the fourteenth day arrived, they would take the sheep and move them. In the second phase, when a little warmth appeared, there was no more need. In the third phase, the warmth inside the earth grew.

The trees that bear fruit: The first is called 'al-Ajuz' (the Old Woman), which is seven days. At the beginning of those days, the trees bear fruit, the air is clean, and the wind blows gently. As is natural, the cold intensifies at the end and the lamp flickers; one should sit sheltered and not venture out into the cold. The creatures move and the insects emerge. These are the 'Days of the Old Woman.' It is said that in these days, the tribe of 'Ad was destroyed, and from them remained an old woman (ajuz), after whom these days are named. These days are remembered and called 'The Days of the Old Woman (Ayyam al-Ajuz).'

The cold intensifies; the swift (khattaf) arrives; life becomes confined. For as long as the cold and darkness last, the earth remains inhabited and people stay within. The grain field of wheat ripens with close attention, and whoever watches the stars and does not sleep — it is said the woman will bear children and the wheat will turn fragrant in it, the legumes ripen, and in a healthy condition all is well.

From the first day onward, there is hope for rain. The auspicious day will be counted. There will be an eastern wind, intense cold, and the birds will begin to nest; in Palestine, the south wind (habub) blows greatly, and its blowing is very great. The almond tree bears fruit, the fruit decreases, the north wind brings cold, and the Nile of Egypt increases greatly. 

In the era of the Caliphs in Baghdad: there is a decrease in the Nile of Egypt; the cold in the land increases. The nights are at their shortest and the days are at their longest. Wheat and other grain prices decrease. Zechariah (Zakariyya) was born, and his son [Yahya/John] likewise. When [the water] increases, it is greenish in color. On this day, if one sees many birds flying in pairs making their way, the Nile extends and does not recede. The herders drive their cattle to pasture, flowers bloom on the fields, and all kinds of plants and grasses spread across the land, and the animals rest in their pastures.

On the Knowledge of the Months

When the rays of that night rise upon that tree, then the days of paradise will have passed and it will come to pass that night — a luminous star will appear upon it. If it is green, then the crops and seeds of that year will prosper and arms will come in abundance. Whatever has turned yellow indicates that in that year there will be hardship and the beginning of destruction, and affairs will turn toward misfortune. These are the first days of Muharram. There are seven days, and each day indicates the condition of one of the months — from this they make inferences about weather changes and so on. They say these days correspond to the year in terms of illness and each day indicates blood. If it is dry and hot, there will be plagues; if crops are planted in winter and the trees are trimmed, the fruits will be abundant. The colors of the citrus will change at the end and the year will be troubled, and dates and fresh fruits will be affected. They say the market will be slow and the food prices will rise, cold water will come down and hot will be scarce. In the beginning it was established that the children and young ones would find the season of equilibrium between night and day — that is Nowruz, the first of the year. On this day one should purify one's soul and body, and treat illnesses. New branches will appear on the known trees, and many crows will be seen. Chapter on the Persian months: They are equal in number to three hundred and six days per year, and the names of their months are: the days of Hormuz, Bahman, Ordibehesht, Shahrivar, Esfandaramaz, Abad, Azar, Khur, Mah, Tir, Khosh, Vahram, Srosh, Ramesh, Farvardin, Haram, Laram, Vauobandadin, Din Ardad, Vashtao, Jahan, Ramiyad, Mah, Esfand — and these are the Iranian months according to the Farsi calendar. The first day of every month is called Nowruz, meaning the first of Farvardin, which is the first of the year. It is said that on this day God chose the archangel Gabriel and said: 'O Gabriel, the angel of revelation is the messenger of God.' The Persians say that on this day fortune attends whoever works; the first action of the day is weighing and measuring — and if one does good deeds on this day, every action will be blessed. The third of Ordibehesht is called Ardibehesht and is a festival of the holy fire-worshippers, called by the name of that day's angel, and it is a celebrated occasion. On this day it is established by tradition and those before have ordained it so. The sixth day is called Khordad and its festival is Khordad — and this is one of the days of harmony with the name of Zarathustra's institution. The first of the next period, the fourth, is also celebrated; on this day the trees bear good fruit and it is called the day of the freshwater springs. On this day people sprinkle cold water on each other. The sixth...

On the Knowledge of Months
[Page] 48

It is called Gharah. When the new month begins, on Wednesday it is also called the feast day of the Turks, because its name is associated with livestock. They slaughter [animals] and say that on this day Manuchehr asked for the realm of Iran to be given to him, and Zav accepted and gave Iran to Manuchehr. Manuchehr fortified himself in Tabaristan. This day is called Mihr-ruz [the Day of Mihr]. They also say that on this day Afridun received his first revenge. On the sixteenth of every month, the day of Mihr is a great feast, and they call it Harkhan. From that time on, the sun was upon it, and on this day it is said that the dome was [placed]. Before sitting upon the throne, while striking down [the enemy], and so it is said that when Kaveh the blacksmith aided in the cause, the day was devoted to this...

[Marginalia: The word Kaveh the Fifth / the digging of the earth]

In the year when the throne was established, Zahhak was overcome by Fereydun; Fereydun captured him and Zahhak said to Fereydun: "Destroy me." Fereydun agreed and with twelve [companions] constructed [the celebration], and that day became a feast, hence the agreement. And the people of Aban called this day, saying that on this day the construction of the land, its rivers and streams, spread across the climes. This day is called Lomba [?]. On this day the spirits of the great are lasting, and on the first of each Hormoz [day] they say that on the day of Karaj the nobles would eat warm foods, would keep themselves in order, and the people showed mercy to one another and among the great, from each person they took something; and if someone did not give, a great conquest would come upon them. They sought a vessel and a ring and dishes, and they say that on this day [things] are given by way of custom and fortune. Whoever on this day seeks counsel before travelling, let them take a quince and a turnip for the whole year to be prosperous. This is one of the remembered days and it is a feast; it is called Azarjashn [the Fire Festival], fires are lit and it is said that Zardosht declared that on this day the fires are kindled.

On the Knowledge of the Month of Bahman

They call this month also the month of Ahsram, and also the day of Haram. The fire dies down, and on this day one should wear white garments and ride a white horse, and lift the veil, and occupy oneself with the subjects. And whoever desires — whether high or low — let him be generous. The artisans and farmers should sit together, and the king should say: I know that the stability of the world depends on cultivation and agriculture, and I am like two brothers who are grateful. On this day of celebration and justice, cook meat and offer it as a gift; on this day milk is bought and sold. On this day they make figures of copper and clay, and honor them as royal houses. Fire is kindled on this day, and poetry is composed about how whoever celebrates this day will be free from all troubles for the year, and whoever honors this day will be safe and joyful. This is proclaimed by the people. At the beginning of this blessed day of Bahman, the second day is a day of rest and rejoicing, and the people of Persia on this day prepare watermelons and all kinds of meats, and drink milk. They say that on this day eating these things is especially beneficial. It is said this is the day of Eid, and from it a hundred days of winter pass. And some say this is the day when winter ends. The people light fires, cook food, kings roast birds over the fire, and fish are grilled; they light fires in open spaces and fields so that the flames of the fire may be seen everywhere. As for the thirtieth day, in Isfahan the bakers would go, and Nushirwan's reign was prosperous: he abolished the collection of tribute, distributed the goods of the treasury among the people, forbade anyone to be left homeless, and said: 'My intention is to look after my subjects. If I am merciful, and if I punish wrongdoing, then...' And the rains came and the people rejoiced, as no one in that era had seen such rain. The people were glad and came out of their houses celebrating, and this tradition of rejoicing has continued from that time.

Esfand: Among the days of this month, the day of Shahrivar is a day of celebration and justice. From the break of dawn, letters of request are written and placed on the walls of the house, facing the main wall. This day is also called the day of the Great Men, meaning that on this day women choose their husbands. The first is good, and the second: it is said that God Almighty created water on this day in Farvardin. On this day they kindle fires and waters flow. Physicians prescribe medicines on this day.

On the Seasons of the Year:

When the sun reaches the point of Aries, spring begins. When it reaches Libra, autumn begins. When it reaches Capricorn, winter begins. And when it returns to Aries, spring begins again — God Almighty having made it so that each season brings its own qualities, agreeable or disagreeable.

On the Knowledge of Months

Another quality is that the transitions toward the seasonal turning-points happen gradually, except where the two qualities oppose each other, as for example when mid-winter resembles summer. From that point on, a great transformation takes place in the weather — consider how some days are warm and others cold. How wonderful and great is His design, and how gracious His bounty! As for Nawruz (the New Year) and the equinox: the weather becomes temperate, the air pleasant, a gentle breeze blows, the cold melts away, the valleys fill with water, and flowers bloom everywhere; streams and rivers run full, trees put out leaves, the earth turns green with plants and small creatures appear and scatter across the ground. The earth is adorned, and this continues until the first of Aries.

As for Summer: the length of day increases and the nights grow short; the earth grows warm, plants and saplings flourish, trees bear fruit, livestock mate, and people enjoy the season's bounty, as is well observed. Its beginning is when the sun enters Libra, day and night are equal, the sea calms, and the rivers become gentle — until the sun enters Capricorn, at which point winter begins.

As for Autumn: its beginning is when the sun reaches the first of Capricorn; the nights grow long and the days short. After this, the cold intensifies, plants wither, leaves fall from trees, and the air becomes contrary — so that whoever spent the summer in cool places now seeks heat in winter. The old saying holds: the wheel turns, and lifespans are consumed, until the sun returns to the first of Aries.

Chapter on the Wonders That Occur
Some scholars say that God the Exalted sends a messenger with miracles every thousand years, to make religion manifest. This means that every thousand years there may be an interval of a millennium, or even less. Thus the first thousand years saw Adam, father of humanity; the second, Noah; the third, Abraham; the fourth, Moses; the fifth, Jesus; and the sixth, Muhammad the Chosen, God's blessings upon him — with whom prophecy was sealed and perfection completed. It is reported on authority that six thousand years have passed, then seven thousand, then eight thousand, then nine thousand, then ten thousand — and at the head of every hundred years God brings forth a scholar to renew the faith. [The author then lists a chain of scholars.] It is related from Anas ibn Malik, raised to the Prophet (peace be upon him), that he said: whoever lives to sixty years, God softens his heart; whoever lives to seventy, God makes him an intercessor for his household; whoever lives to ninety, God forgives his sins and he becomes God's protector on earth among his family.

Scholars also say: extraordinary and strange things reappear periodically, and remarkable events manifest themselves in the world — such as intense heat followed by intense cold, the drying of seas, the appearance of strange plants and animals unlike anything known. Let this discussion suffice, and now we turn to wonderful and strange tales.

Anecdote:
There was a young man among the Children of Israel who had come to know the ways of Islam and longed for the company of the wise. One day, as fate would have it, the young man set out seeking knowledge, saying: 'I have heard that Khidr (peace be upon him) comes to you — is this so?' The young man replied: 'Yes.' The king said: 'When Khidr comes to you again, bring him to me so that I may meet him.' The young man replied: 'How can I bring him to you?' The king said: 'If you do not bring him before me, I will have you killed.' At this, the young man fell into anxious thought...

Khidr appeared and the story goes that the angel informed him that a young man had come before the presence [of Khidr], the young man explained his own situation, and Khidr commanded: 'Learn and rise.' He sent a young man with an angel before his presence. When the angel came to him he said that you are in [Khidr's] sight. The angel said: 'Tell me the most wondrous thing you have seen.'

He said: 'How wonderful — I have seen many things, but at this very moment let me tell you. I came to a very populous and well-built city. I asked one of the people about the state of that city. After another long period of years I passed by another place — it had become a sea, and fishermen were catching fish. I asked one of them: 'When did this land become a sea?' He said: 'Someone like you asks such a question? This land used to be a battlefield.' He said: 'I saw it [before], yet I had not witnessed this.' The king said: 'I wish to follow you.' [Khidr] said: 'You cannot follow me, but follow this young man, who will guide you toward good and away from evil, and he will be a comfort to you.' In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate — and God alone grants right guidance. Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds.

The Second Discourse: On the Lower World (Sublunar Realm)
And everything that derives from the heavenly spheres, consisting of the elements and composite things. The first section concerns the true nature of the elements, which are the fundamental principles of all things. The king proclaimed: 'The mothers (primary elements) are water, air, fire, and earth. As for the compounds that arise from these mothers...'

On the Sphere (Section 52)

Plants and animals [come] first. Fire, by its natural place, is just below the celestial sphere, and air is the natural place of fire, being below fire and above water. Water's natural place is below air and above earth, and earth's natural place is in the middle. By the perfect wisdom of the Almighty, He arranged the elements in a wondrous way: whatever is lighter is closer to the celestial sphere, and whatever is heavier is farther from it. Fire, being the lightest, adheres closest [to the sphere], and earth, being the heaviest of all, is at the greatest distance. Air is heavier than fire but lighter than water, so its natural place is below the sphere of fire and above the sphere of water. Water is heavier than air but lighter than earth, so its natural place is above earth and below the sphere of air.

Second observation on the sphere: when a body that has form transforms—as when air becomes water, as is observed when droplets appear on the surface of water—it becomes clear that they have gathered from the air. This happens from extreme coldness, causing the air and water to condense. Similarly, it is seen in poisonous places where heat exists, and as is seen from iron-smelting furnaces: when the tongs are brought near [the furnace], the air around them transforms, and if something is brought close, water forms from the ground—as some people say who live near iron mines, where water gathers. Among these phenomena is that when water flows in a curved channel, pure sweet water rises from it.

The sphere of fire is simple and pure in nature, and its nature demands that it move until it settles just below the celestial sphere. Fire has no color, and the proof of this is that when pure fire in a furnace gives its full heat to something brought near it—like iron brought to a forge—nothing [of its own color] appears in it. The fire above is purer than what is below it. By the craft of the Almighty, the lower part of the celestial sphere is such that it refines the dense vapors that rise up like smoke, making them subtle and transparent—like a single layer spread in all directions so that whatever arises is immediately refined. Otherwise, those dense vapors would obstruct the sight of the celestial world. So He made [the sphere of fire] a barrier against blocking the view of the earth. Otherwise, if it were not there, the elements of animal and plant life would be consumed and destroyed.

Glory be to God Most High! What a wondrous thing more remarkable than this: that the essence of light dwells between iron and stone, both of which are dense, yet it emerges. And if it were not that every day and night each thing were drawn together—if someone were to collect it, the heaviness of the accumulation would be a wonder. And more wondrous still is that from a green tree—which by its appearance should contain water—fire is produced. As He the Most High has said: 'He who made for you from the green tree fire, and from it you kindle.' So consider, the power of the Sultan [God] who—like grain being threshed—destroys the exalted and annihilates the iron that was struck. For the most solid things are never truly permanent, and their soundness passes. As for the wonderful fires of the Children of Israel: the fire that remained unharmed through every trial was such that it would not burn what it touched.

On the Knowledge of the Sphere

There was a sacrificial offering in that place, and in that house there were sounds and a keeper, and the people of that house were... white descended from the sky, and this is what God the Exalted has informed us — 'Those who said: we will not believe in the messenger until he brings us a gift' — and it came down from the sky like a strange wonder, sharp as silk.

In those lands it appeared as if illuminated, brightening from within, so that its days and being were: when the ruby-like essence emerged from within and came close to the fire, it was nourishing and the room was lit until Khalid ibn Shaban sent it — together with Moses — as an ambassador to all, glorified, and he departed.

[Section heading:] On Shooting Stars and Comets

They say that when smoke rises into the air and reaches upward until the sphere [of fire] is encountered and the heat intensifies — so that the sphere of fire ignites it — then the smoke that rises from the lower sphere, when it reaches the fiery zone, becomes ignited and light. If that smoke is of a pure fiery nature, thin and fine, it burns like pure fire, moving swiftly. If it resembles quicksilver in shape, it takes the form of the inner smoke. When it separates, it takes the form seen across the surface of the heavens. This is a summary of that truth.

[Section heading:] The Third Layer — The Sphere of Air

The sphere of air: air is described as moist, warm, transparent, located below the sphere of fire and above the sphere of water, according to the philosophers who came before. Because of the revolution of the celestial sphere and the speed of its rotation, the sphere of air — from the pure fire downward — becomes heated, and that part is called the first division. The second division: through the reflection of solar rays bouncing off the surface of the earth, the air becomes temperate — and this is called the middle section. This is like the reflection of water on the surface of the earth, which is cold. The part beneath the north pole, where the sun does not shine, where it is far from the sun and the sky is dark — there plants do not grow. They say the sphere [of air] is six thousand three hundred leagues [in extent]. The mountain heights in that region: the heat is concentrated there because the barriers that prevent loss of heat — namely, the air current from the earth's surface and the reflection of rays from the ground — are absent there. When one climbs high and the needed air current does not reach [from below], it is like a lamp with no air: the flame goes out, because living beings cannot breathe without air. This is why a lamp placed there goes out, and a living creature suffocates.

[Section heading:] On the Causes of Rain

They say that when sunlight strikes the earth, moisture is dissolved from water and soil — this dissolved vapor is what they call 'smoke' or vapor from the earth. As this vapor rises and the air carries it upward until it reaches a cold region, it condenses by royal decree [of nature], and from the upper cold comes [the frost]. It penetrates the mountains and accumulates, continuously joining together until it thickens and forms what is called a cloud. When clouds accumulate and gather densely, the material precipitates and falls — and there...

On the Knowledge of Wind

Water then divides into portions, and drops gather together, then they aim downward. After that the vapor rises, and if the air is cold, it prevents penetration and congeals, and it becomes fine, and in other than snow it forms, because it is the substance of a liquid that becomes frozen, and it mixes with the air and clouds form, and afterward hail descends. If the air is low, the vapor rises and condenses, and layer upon layer forms, two or three layers accumulating, each one above the other, and they pile up layer by layer, and the drops become heavy and descend. If the descent is extreme, hail forms; and if much cold air is present, bubbles form; and if it is thin, it becomes dew; and if warm below and very cold above, frost forms, and it weakens. One who understands these conditions and verifies them will comprehend how the water in the bath-house ceiling drips, and why in some places the ceiling drips — as is known to occur at fixed and known times in Iran each year, and there is proof of this. For a young man in Iran it is beneficial, and the spring causes such striking of every place between them — from forty stages down the water flows, and it cannot make a station, since the drop lands there and it sets in motion what is sufficient to send to the farthest place. Not a single plant there reaches completion, and it does not approach the provision from the sky: "He sent down from the sky water" and "He sent down" — for the account of the chapter:

On Winds: Wind is such that the air surges and moves in waves, and it is composed of subtle parts — these subtle parts are the cause of their being seen coming, coming from the warming of the sun on the earth's surface, rising up from the ground; and when the gentle warmth of the surface becomes hot and dry, it seeks to descend, and the air surges, and this is like a master who knows: just as one who throws something onto the surface of water produces movement, so too the air begins to move when the heat comes and the wave strikes, and the expert on this says that it returns in layers. The clouds grow intense and become vapors, and their movement collides with one another, and when they fall the air also moves, and two opposing movements collide and neither prevents the other, and so it goes. And from this comes what is seen — the winds strike and the rains fall and the clouds shine, and the sources and origins of winds: to the north and south and their blowing places, and the sound from the plain. The North wind, however, blows between the rising of the North and the East — that is, between the northeast; and the South wind blows between the plain and the West — that is, the Southwest. Understand it thus: the sun's rays reach the pores of the air and there the snow and severe cold remain; because when it flows there it accepts the cold, and in that direction the desert winds are cool, and among the mountains on every side winds come out — just as someone throws a breath inward, and against the South the vast plain extends. The North wind is praised and the South condemned. The North makes the constitution strong, clears the brain, purifies the temperament, makes the heart good, and sharpens the sight. In many animals the North wind is better. Among the Arabs, however, the North is considered disagreeable, and they say it brings hardship — but the South delights the spirit...

On the Knowledge of Thunder and Lightning

It happens that the blowing winds come from the direction of Khata [Central Asia], and there the heat is intense because of the sun, which is in that place for two seasons per year. In spring it senses south [wind] and brings it along. The best condition occurs when it turns the air and reduces what is in the north, decreasing [the cold] there, so that just as the south [wind] makes things cold, the reason given for this is that when the water is warm and the north wind brings coldness into it, the heat enters from outside, and just as one sees in winter how the earth's inner heat comes out and mixes above, so the south [wind] brings the inner heat of the water to the outside, just as one sees in summer how the heat comes from inside the earth. When the heat rises, the nature of water, being cold by nature, returns to its own nature and keeps perspiration well contained. The physicians say this, and they say: if Saba [the east wind] blows, it is a wind close to moderation. If during the day effort is made, it will have gathered the good things from the distant regions of the horizon, having been settled during the nighttime, and at that time the Saba wind is extremely pleasant—except that since the sun's rays go before it and moderate and refine [the air], and establish its equilibrium, for this reason it is called the morning [wind], because people enjoy it, the sick find relief at that time of night, and one enjoys half the night from it. The Dabur [west wind], which opposes the Saba, blows at the time when the Saba's direction of blowing has been left behind, and as it reaches the end of the day it strikes those in front and behind, for the horizons have passed from its direction of blowing, and at every time that it blows it comes.

Chapter on Thunder and Lightning: It is believed that as a physician determined, when the wind is stopped—as described—and is confined in a cloud, if the wind then tries to escape by its own force, and if it breaks through and tears the cloud and disperses it, the sound of thunder comes from it. If the fine [lightning] appears, it is because when elements of opposing natures collide, some fire ignites within, and lightning flashes forth; if it is fine [in texture] it becomes a thunderbolt. If it is dense, it descends and, as mentioned, reaches the sea, and the south [wind] makes it blow away. If it falls on a mountain it strikes the rocky crags and blows them away, so that the water that falls there blazes up, and lightning occurs before thunder, both arising together—yet lightning is seen before thunder is heard, because sight reaches [us] and the gatherings of air and their arrival at the hearing and the centers of sound do not reach [us] immediately, like someone clapping a garment beside a sea: the flash is seen at once, but the sound reaches [us] only some time later. Thunder-companions and lightning do not arise [simply] because the smoky vapors rise—by virtue of the extreme cold and just as hoarfrost arises—and lightning arises thus.

Chapter on the Halo, the Rainbow, and the Arc: Know that the rainbow and the arc depend on several premises, and when those premises are understood, the matter will be clarified afterward. The first premise: know that reflection [of light] cannot be perceived without [the principle of] inversion, because true reflection does not occur on the outside in reality, and [ordinary] reflection does not truly exist on the outside either—rather it is assumed [to be so]. It is not [a matter of] confusion between the two types of reflection: when the reflection of light is understood, the reflection of vision is established on this basis. The reflection of light occurs in such a way that a ray from a physical, polished body is reflected in luminous [matter] and another body becomes revealed, on the condition that its position from this...

On the Knowledge of the Body of the Sun

As a fortunate body, the position of this luminous body becomes connected and contrary, and in it there appears a concavity such that it connects with another, as if joined. This is to say that from the earth the essence becomes known and revolves around the body's surface, and around the line of the hand of the sun's rays. When it is contrary to the direction of the sun, the rays return from the mirrors and from the mirrors back, and the body reveals the line in that direction toward the sun, and from the mirrors and rays return from the mirrors back, and the body reveals it — as if among them there is no carrier, and the increase is the greatest.

Where the ray and the perpendicular line stand upright upon the surface of the mirror, as a vertical line upon the surface, if we draw a line upon it, it becomes apparent from the observation that this is the ray, and from it, as it is assumed upon the surface of the mirror, the angle and from the line along which the ray returns — there is the other angle — it becomes apparent that it is parallel to the preceding angle, and it is the angle of the separation of the ray and the reflection of the ray. And when we assume that the perpendicular ray line becomes the condition of the mirror, the reflection does not exist — it returns to itself.

From these premises it becomes known what the ray is, what the reflected ray is, and what the returning ray is, and accordingly it becomes necessarily understood that the reflection originates from the surface — wherever we assume it, if we draw a line from this point toward the east and contrary to the direction of the observer, and if we arrange it thus — just as the line of the observer is drawn, this is revealed: in this way these lines are not spent, and the observer's origin and the angle of reflection is what people call the mirror. As it has been said: if a person considers and responds, the first answer would be that it is elevated; accordingly, the conditions of the second premise are that if the mirror is small, it is called the reflected image of the world — whatever is outside is primary. The third premise: if the mirror has color, the color of light passing through it to the foundation will spread, and if it is white and without color, and likewise if the fourth premise is present — which is the position and location — then other transformations of position occur, and truly the arrangement and determination of the location of the observer is such that these premises become known.

[Page number:] 31

On the Knowledge of Waters

It is said regarding the phenomenon known to the people of Hadhramaut: a rainbow-like luminous form appears in the air, which is a fine, subtle medium that, like a transparent screen, does not allow sunlight to pass through directly; instead, the light is reflected within it. When a body of a particular position and composition intercepts the rays, the color becomes reddish. If the body is small, then any form can be observed within it. Thus every part of that medium, being luminous, forms a bright circle, and from this emerges what is known as the Rainbow.

The explanation is as follows: contrary to the direction of the sun, when fine, transparent droplets or mist hang in the air — and the eye's ray, reflected from these droplets back toward the sun, passes through these mist particles — the rays of sight are reflected from that medium, and from those particles in the direction opposite the sun, the colors of the spectrum emerge, because the light, meeting these particles, yields colors, just as in a prism. When the medium consists of fine particles, every one of those particles shows a hue and shape — red, green, yellow, and other colors of varying intensities — thus the colors are seen in different gradations. If the medium is more transparent, sunlight penetrates through and the rainbow is formed. I observed the rainbow not merely as a mental image but in reality, and its position is such that it appears to carry light by reflection.

A wise Muslim scholar remarked: the cause and nature of this phenomenon is such that every worthy authority has discussed it. And the image it produces is like a reflection in still water. The Shaykh al-Ra'is [Avicenna] said: there is a mountain in the land of Tus of tremendous height; one day the sky was clear, and I was between the mountain and the flat plain. The surface of the mountain received sunlight, and from that position — me standing between the mountain and the ground — I could see a full rainbow. In the hope of reaching it, I started walking from the mountain downward toward the valley, and as I descended I found the circle growing smaller. When I finally reached the flat ground, the circle had entirely disappeared.

Section Four: On the Sphere of Water — it is said thus:

Water's natural place is below the air and above the earth, and it is said its shape is spherical; for if a sailor climbs a mountain, when he first reaches the summit he can see the surface of the sea is convex — because closer mountains and wide plains are visible — and the nearer one approaches the water the less of it one can see. This demonstrates that the surface of water is curved like a sphere.

The Almighty willed that some part of the earth be exposed, because the noblest type of creation — human beings — needs to live on the land. Thus it is said that most aquatic creatures live in water, while land creatures live on the ground, each suited to its element. The divine wisdom arranged matters such that the sphere of water does not fully cover the sphere of earth, so that the surface of the earth is partly exposed and creatures may live upon it.

Water is of two kinds: salt water and fresh water. In each kind there are benefits. Salt water supports sea creatures. The reason the sea is salty is that the sun's heat acts upon it, evaporating the pure water and leaving behind the salt — for if the sea were fresh, the influence of the sun would make it putrid, and the vapors rising from it would spread disease in the surrounding air, and plagues would destroy living creatures. Divine wisdom therefore ordained that the sea should be salty, so that it would not become corrupted. Among the benefits of the sea's saltiness are that within it grow ambergris and coral and other things of value. As for fresh water, its greatest benefit is nourishment and the sustenance of all living creatures.

On the Subject of the Seas

God Most High, in His wisdom, made the oceans such that their nature and color are fixed and constant. Just as a young person's constitution is by nature vigorous, so too, through God's grace, human beings attain their full potential. Unlike other foods, beverages, and edibles whose benefits depend on digestion, the water of the sea — though salty — has been made so by the Almighty, who in His great kindness has removed its harshness. Through the evaporation of sea water, vapors rise and are carried to whatever location is desired, bringing water to springs, rivers, mountains, and valleys. Indeed, each season has its proper measure. 

Chapter on Maritime Affairs and the Wonders of the Sea: On the conditions of the sea, the rise and fall of its waters, tides, the variation of its times according to the four seasons, the months, the hours of day and night, and the causes of the rising of waters — all of this occurs because when the sun moves away and grows gentle, it warms a certain place, causing the water to rise there. From the four directions — east, west, north, and south — the air moves over the shores, and at times different winds blow. The sea rocks like a bowl: when the sun strikes the surface of the sea and its rays reflect off the water, the water grows warm and light. Warm water, being more buoyant than cold water, causes waves to rise. Some of the water is pushed toward the shore while some is driven deeper. This continues until the sun reaches the middle of the sky — the meridian — at which point these motions cease, and the waters settle. Sometimes the body produces excess bile, which gradually accumulates. To put it more elegantly: God has appointed an angel over the sea, whose robe trails along its surface, and from the sea arise islands and creatures — the marvels of the Encompassing Sea.

This sea surrounds all the other seas; it encompasses the entire world. The Greeks called it 'Okeanos,' and Ka'b al-Ahbar and others have said that God Most High created seven seas. The first is the Encompassing Ocean, which lies around the whole earth like a ring, and it is called Tunbash. Then comes another sea named Abam, and a fourth called Admaras, and a fifth named Udak. All four oceans are together. This sea — the one people know as the weak sea — is in truth that very sea. From it, God has fashioned rivers, animals, crocodiles, and creatures. Khwarazmians say that the people of that sea call it 'the Encompassing' and that the Greeks call it the Ocean. Those who dwell on its shores pass along it, but no one crosses its middle, for if one ventures out to sea, one disappears. The Greeks say it is impassable. Near its shores are rocks, and to the south and north it faces Rum (Rome/Byzantium) and Bulgaria, and going further, one exits toward the pole. From there the sea opens up, and one travels toward the east. Between its shores, as far as the most distant lands of the Turks and beyond, there are very many places, and some are ruined — no one has come back from there.

On the Pages of the Seas
59

The dwelling place, know that going eastward one reaches the great Gulf that comes out of the China Sea, which is among the most famous of gulfs. The first is the Gulf of China, which is also called the Sea of Hind, from which the Gulf of Qulzum extends, going on until it reaches Aden, then continues to the strait of the Sea, and in this sea of Paks the navigation is dangerous. Then it extends to the place called the Ropes, which is the source of the Nile of Egypt, and from there it extends to the Land of the Sudan in the west, and from there to the lands of Ankas and the sea, and in this sea there are islands whose count only God the Almighty knows, and each island is about twenty farsakhs or two farsakhs or a farsakh, and among the most famous of the islands are Qiyus, Samos, Rhodes, and Sicily, and to the south of these islands are the islands known as Madhib and Socotra. In Bahjat al-Afaq, Samarqandi relates that I read in certain accounts that Dhu al-Qarnayn wished to circumnavigate the shores of the sea, so he ordered a ship to travel for a full year so as to bring news of the shores of this sea. The ship departed for a year and found no shore, then it turned back. When it returned, it was found that a fish — a Chinese fish — was known to others, and some went to the water and a ship appeared with people aboard. One of them spoke in a language that Dhu al-Qarnayn's interpreter could understand, and among them was a woman. When she was brought before Dhu al-Qarnayn, she said: we come from a place where the mother's tongue and the father's tongue are spoken. She said: Why have you come here? She said: Our king Lalamak sent us to see the conditions of the neighboring lands. They said: In our country there is a king far greater than your king and more desirous and with far more people, and by the power of God the Almighty, glory be to Him...

[Illustration: The image of Dhu al-Qarnayn and the people of the island]

Note: God alone knows best. The Sea of China — the Sea of Chin is connected to the Sea of Khata and the Sea of Basij, and nearby is the encircling ocean. Many waves rise and fall there. It is said that when the Sea of China desires to move, it gathers momentum like a torrent, and then, as Abu Rayhan [al-Biruni] says, when it is about to move it becomes calm, and those who wish to reach its shore and remain always in the depths of the sea should know that when it becomes calm, in this sea there are special forms. Know that from the time the sea becomes calm, in this sea there are particular images and within it...

On the Page of the Island of Ir

It is known that in these regions there are mineral deposits of gold, and some of the islands have mines of great wealth, and the animals found there are of strange and unusual forms. There is an island called Dai, which has a chest-cavity that opens and the body becomes visible from outside. On the Description of Rivers and Canals
(page 113)

This text, drawn from classical Persian cosmographical tradition, discusses various rivers and canals, particularly in Iraq and Egypt. The following is a summary translation of the key passages:

The author recounts how certain rivers were dug by order of Khosrow (Kisra, the Sassanid emperor), including the canal known as Nahr al-Ghatoun (the Ghatoun River), which was excavated for irrigation and public benefit. It is noted that when Khosrow came and exercised his authority, he ordered this canal constructed so that water could be drawn from it for cultivation across the land.

The text then describes Baghdad and its famous landmarks, mentioning the ʿAyn al-Mulk (Eye of the Kings), a celebrated spring or well in Baghdad, said to have been established or blessed in the time of Solomon, and over which various communities had claims and disputes.

The passage moves on to Egypt and the Nile. It describes how Yusuf (Joseph) and scholars measured the Nile's flood levels. A nilometer (miqyas) was established to gauge the annual flood: when the water reached a certain height, the people would rejoice and begin cultivation. If the Nile reached nineteen cubits (dhiraʿ), the harvest would be good; if it rose higher, to twenty cubits, the return would be fourfold. The scholars of Egypt used these measurements to advise the population on the extent and quality of the annual harvest, and the people would accordingly pay their dues and plan their agricultural activities based on the level recorded on the nilometer.

Chapter Nine: On the Properties of These Things

Yusuf Sadiq said: The reason for its mention and the chapter on the sword is that this work brings together the pain of longing. In those lands, great rains come at the beginning of spring until they reach Egypt, but when it is summer, the need for agriculture at that time is such. This is the arrangement of natural wisdom. What has been mentioned of animals has passed, and the weavings and strange animals are of the finest kind. People do not go near the banks of the Nile out of fear of crocodiles, and in the Nile there are places where enormous numbers of fish gather, and the people there catch and take great quantities of fish every day throughout the year, and the same happens again the following year; the people there never tire of it. A thousand riders and a thousand footmen pass by it, and a thousand views of it are seen from afar. These women who are kept away and separated from men would lose their minds. The author of Tuhfat al-Gharaib says: When the sun rises in the east, it sets in the west, and when it sets the traveler goes east.

Chapter on the Generation of Springs and Waters: How they enter through cracks and openings, whether by air or water. If it is air, it flows and moves quickly, and when the eagle swoops down it is attracted to that side of the land. If the land is hard, the treatment is to bring in pure water; if the land is soft, one builds with earth and water and maintains it. The reason for the variation in springs is that some waters come from them, some are cold: in winter the heat goes underground, and in summer it rises, because in one place the heat gathers together and in some places there is warmth due to the heat of the earth in winter, and when the gathering of that place is complete, the heat becomes pervasive. If it remains permanently in a place and there is no opening on the west side, or the heat builds up and the earth purifies, the flow from the surface of the earth will be warm, or if it is directed, or if it is pointed it will attract contraries and others, and it will be forced out by pressure. The author of Tuhfat al-Gharaib says regarding Azerbaijan: there is a spring there, and its water is very fierce; most people try it and become ill, and it kills those who come late to it. The spring of Ardamahshak is between two towns, six parasangs distant. When a person drinks it, it purges them severely. There are special properties to it; it is worth going to and spending the night near. Every year in spring, people come from Qarnun and other places to drink it, and when one brings water from al-Qarnun and mixes it with the water of Ardamahshak, the property of the Ardamahshak water is nullified. This is in the land of Sistan, and there the water flows over hard stone, and beyond it there is reed-water. The author of Tuhfat al-Gharaib says: Between Asfalnin and Jurjan there is a wonderful thing: in that region there is a cave with a spring in it whose water is somewhat muddy. Some people who were paralyzed were cured at certain times, and people from those towns, men and women and the afflicted, come to it and make vows there and dance and the water flows. Iskandar's spring is famous there. In that place there is a type of shell, large like a melon, and when the broth of it is drunk it cures leprosy. In that place at all times one finds shells, and the author says it has numerous and great benefits.

Description of the Spring with the Face of the Eye

It is said: Those who describe it say that when a person wishes to find the right time and moment, and this is among those [springs], and from them water comes out, and whoever drinks from it their fever-sickness is cured, and from that water something is taken, and when it departs from there, a person who drinks from it — in between, the owner of the Tuhfat al-Gharab says that on the earth, or between the eyes of a spring, the water flows outward, and its urge brings forth — the smell from that water is like sulfur, and if one washes with that water it cures mange. If one takes from that water and pours it in the ear, the hearing becomes clear. One may mention the crimson [spring] — it is said to be a Muslim [spring]. And this place has been described — they say that the water of this spring comes from the Hajj — the owner of the Tuhfat al-Gharab says that this spring is in the region of Itab, and in summer it is extremely cold and in winter extremely warm. A delightful anecdote: a merchant traveled to one of these springs and found its water valuable — whoever comes near it, animals approach it and drink from it without difficulty, and it becomes hard. It is like a blessed spring of the Holy Land. People say from that water the spring of Abraham — now understand this quality: it is a known and well-known thing. This spring's path: if anyone enters it and among the green plants goes into it, the water gushes and expels [impurities], until it becomes clarified and pure. They say that the spring called Fasir and Raq — they say that it has many springs in its interior, very warm, and sometimes it turns red, yellow, green, and white, and from that water pools fill up, especially for the inhabitants. Another spring: they say when a person goes into it, it is beneficial. And the spring called 'Ayn al-Zar'a, east of Mosul — they say it has two springs, dark water, and within it one hears pleasant sounds. Its elevation is [notable]. From its elevation: these two springs — the water is dark. Within it pleasant sounds are heard, and the elevation rises. They say whoever is young and enters this water, whatever wound or sore or paralysis or lameness they have — when they come out, God willing, they are healed and restored. People from that direction come purposely [to this spring]. Like black musk — the owner of the Tuhfat al-Gharab says: from it a mouthful [of water] — and there is a thread-like spring nearby, and people take the water and drink from it, and whoever drinks it warm, it is beneficial. And the spring called 'Ayn Samir — it is the name of a region between Shiraz and Isfahan, and there is a brackish spring there, like hot water — when you see it in summer, water flows from that spring and spreads across the ground there, and in that place one stores and keeps [things] — it is like a treasury. And the people who go to that region drink from it and bathe.

This is the way of the elder of Sanjad:
With this journey of discipline,
From the young ones of this [place],
A bird that is called Suda,
It is called after difficulty,
From every [place] its wisdom did not go away.

On the Description of Its Rivers and Springs

The fig of Zand, and in this property it resembles the olive, as we have seen in Constantinople in the year four hundred and something: after reaching it, that water was sent up, and along the way alone seven springs were found there. Its water has flowed for seven years continuously, such that the region was cut off for seven years and the livestock [perished]. In Qazvin and its environs, 'Abd Allah reported that there a spring exists; from that place warm water rises to the height of a man, and its foam goes forth, and the water flows down like a stream to a place five leagues away, and there it joins a gathering of companions afflicted with illness who come there intentionally. It has been said [regarding] 'Ayn al-'Uqab: in Talā and in Janjana there is a place in whose hills the owner of 'Ajā'ib al-Gharā'ib says that when an eagle grows old and its hunting weakens, they bring it to that spring and bathe it, and it returns to its youth, its feathers renew, and its desire for hunting is restored. And Abu Hamid al-Andalusi says that there is a church there and in it a spring, and the olive trees of the people there are famous and well-known. The people of that place came and found the olive trees turning green and bearing olives, and from those olives and from that estate a garden was planted for the benefit and prosperity of the region. It is said in the cities that the olive [spring] and the place of the olive spring are there, and the river runs near it. It is near Ghazna: if three things depart from there together, the rain will come and the green will appear and will prosper, until when it reaches Mecca it is gathered there. It is said that the Sultan would campaign toward Ghazna, and whoever came there and gathered from that place, and the Sultan could not reach that place and came away; that expeditionary force was sent and that spring was identified. It was said that near the land of Erzurum there is a spring of virtue such that whoever bathes in its spring in spring and summer will be healed of his ailments. [Regarding] 'Ayn Futra: it is said that the people of Khurasan and the doctors of Khurasan recount regarding the special properties of this spring: if a person with quartan fever bathes in this spring, his illness will depart. [Regarding] 'Ayn al-Kilank: this spring is in the region of Khoy, a moderate and beneficial water. [Regarding] al-Mash'ar: it is a small city with a weak spring; the house received visitors four times a day in the morning, and the spirit of God — it is reported that God Almighty commanded that whoever reaches that spring and drinks of its water, a thousand and some will come to him and he will be blessed; and the Blessed Hand was placed upon it and was invoked, and the water flowed, and the people came in great numbers, and from there they went and the people honored it greatly. Abu Rayhan al-Khwarizmi says: I have heard from the people of Marv that in the description of that spring and several [others]: that from there a great army sets out and the land is conquered, and between them the river runs free of obstruction, and the city is a town in which the Sultan Salah al-Din commanded an expedition to that place and returned, and so it remained. 'Ayn — the owner of 'Ajā'ib al-Gharā'ib says: in this place there is a cave and in it a spring whose water flows out, and in that cave there is mud, and the spring gives it moisture, and that mud becomes mice, and someone recounted that he went there and from those mice he was healed, and the spring of that place flows and the owner of 'Ajā'ib al-Gharā'ib says there is a cleft in a mountain, and whoever needs water and comes to that place where the water flows — and it is said that he who returns to [read] this book should look again from the beginning.

On the Description of Rivers and Springs

For when water flows from there for irrigation, and when the need is fully met, one cries out loudly that the water is enough. O Buzrin, cut the lower dam at the spring called 'Ayn al-Haras, which is close by, and that dam and barrier are not far. Thus the water from there comes out in all directions and causes disturbance, and the blood of the strange things that al-Mutawakkil encountered there reached that place. Whatever had been seen, little by little it diminished and the water from there was drawn out greatly, and 'Ayn al-Haras gave water to the district of Nisibis. Its surplus flowed widely, and the scholar of the Book of Wonders of the Regions says that the blood flows through all channels. One went there and spoke of a spring that stood with water full of gems, which would gather every few years, and that director was one of great stature. In that place was a tree of two branches, and those two branches showed that in that spot a virgin had never been seen, so it would appear after many long years. Every day visitors would come and go from those valleys, and the tree would move and there was no one to guard the tree which belonged to the lords of Khorasan and Hyrcan. A person was appointed to watch over that tree day and night until he had the intention, and it happened that four rested there and then one came back to life. The tree had gone and Rafi' was in the middle of the field. At that moment, Hanabsa went and commanded that the means be shown: the tongue of the tree spoke at length and went forward, and it emerged to the extent of a thousand cubits, moving like a leopard. Its water, they say, whoever drinks from it for a thousand cubits, would overcome illness, and whoever comes near it from that place for three days, it would come out with a sound. In between the regions of Rum and Akhlat is a place called Pasi, where there is a spring of great power and a pharmacy. Its sound travels far, and whoever comes near it, all the animals and birds that come around it, large and small — enough of this. The conclusion of the discussion on springs: In the stations of love arranged in ranks, it is renowned for seekers. Whoever drinks the water of those stations, and if someone in those lands says "So-and-so has drunk from them," he is fit for it. And one says near Hajj: I have come, and I affirm, for truly the water of Harut and Marut leads people there.

Chapter Forty-Four
