In the name of God, I went as a pilgrim to those dangerous places — wherever those people were, the Jews argued and debated. Abu Ubayda came, and when he arrived, the Jew said, 'The condition is that neither of us shall invoke the name of God here.' One of them said that both would perish. The Messenger of God — may God's blessings be upon him — had commanded that after one is freed from the blow, God Almighty gave Muslims their due and the polytheists were slain, and in those places the people cast them down, and God commanded a decree upon the inhabitants of the pit. He went and said to 'Utba and Shayba: 'Your faces and your wealth' — and they said, 'O Messenger of God, have you heard their words?' He acted with greater effect. Among us, one of the Muslims said: 'There it is' — and he came out and was seen, and another came out from another side. He came out from outside and gave him a hundred lashes, and again in that pit the news came: 'The great Hajib is at the court of the Prophet — may God's blessings be upon him.' It was said that the spirits of unbelievers are there, and in a valley of great awe. Abraham — peace be upon him — said: 'The worst of the foul valleys, Barhut, is where the souls of unbelievers are gathered.' And it is said that whenever a wind blows from the direction of Barhut and reaches someone, that person falls ill, for it is the wind of the unbelievers' sins spreading through that pure air.

The Messenger of God — peace be upon him — came to this well, performed ablution, and there at the well he rinsed and threw water in. When anyone who has become weak is brought there and drinks that water, he immediately recovers. It is related that some of the people of the west said that from this well a breeze blows outward — if one casts something good into it, it comes back from the bottom with something even better. They threw things into the pit and they came out from beyond — this is a wondrous thing in that island. It is reported that the people of the city sent a rope of five hundred fathoms down and it never reached the bottom. When it came back up, the man said: 'Better than any infidel is what is in this well. I went down and saw a vast and luminous interior, and I saw living and dead people and animals moving about.' This well is a spring of much water, by day and by night, flowing outward endlessly. Whoever comes and looks into it sees it, and it is a blessed place.

Zamzam is the most blessed of wells. It is said that whoever drinks from it if sick is healed; whoever drinks from it if struck by an enemy is saved; and the Commander of the Faithful — may God be pleased with him — commanded 'Abd al-Muttalib. Between sleep and wakefulness 'Abd al-Muttalib was commanded to dig the well of Zamzam. After it had been hidden from sight for some time, a vision came to him. He woke and went forth, and an Arab came to him and said: 'Come and look at this place.' The people of Quraysh came and said that this well had belonged to their forefathers. They agreed upon the land. A soothsayer came from the direction of Syria and told them, and they went. The water was reached with great difficulty — there had been no water there before. When it appeared, 'Abd al-Muttalib praised God and said: 'God has granted this to us.' And the people of Quraysh came and said that this water belongs to us. They agreed. The soothsayer came and adjudicated, and God Most High commanded in accordance with what the soothsayer said. Then 'Abd al-Muttalib departed from Zamzam, went from there to Dhu Anajal, found great abundance and riches. A group came and when he had satisfied the thirst of the pilgrims there, he built a basin for the watering of pilgrims and provided water for the Hajj — and this is why he is called al-Saqib.

This well belongs to your Lord in that land — it is about the distance a horse can travel — and there is a village there called Nazriyya. First, water and good things, and there is a well near Medina, near the settlement between it and the road. The wheat in it grows and the people of the door bring it and distribute it. The narrator of this tale says: I saw this with my own eyes, and my father told me he had heard it, and in those days this news had not yet reached Aaron al-Rashid.

In the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful. This well is in the land of Fars; its depth is several fathoms. It tends to be dry, without moisture rising from it. They say it is like a mill driven by wind. This is the well of which the people of Aleppo say that whoever is sick should come to it; after one day's journey it brings healing, and it is beneficial. And from this well, they say, three men took water and were cured of their ailments.

And they say that in this place, for forty days, the head of the region of Egypt ordered that the balsam trees growing nearby be maintained, and the water of this well mixed with them produces balsam juice. It is said that Jesus entered into this well and prayed, and because of his blessing the balsam tree grows there. Whoever contemplates this well will obtain balsam blood — that is, balsam juice — from the water of this well, because the water within it is of a delicate nature. And I have heard that a certain notable from Kabul came to it and was given permission to draw from the well, and from it water and balsam-blood were obtained.

And balsam is sold in Egypt for great sums. I have heard that scorpions gather around it and no one can approach it; whoever intends to do so is harmed by its spiritual power. And in that town, between two mountains, there is a well from which a fragrant wind blows, and no one can approach it. It is like the well of Joseph — the well into which Joseph was cast. Between fifty and some men tried to visit it and turned back.

On the repulsion of ailments with these wonders...

**On the purpose of examining dense bodies (minerals):**

These are bodies generated from combinations. Bodies that are generated from combinations are either animate or inanimate. If inanimate, they are either mineral or non-mineral. If non-mineral and lacking sensation and movement, they are of a plant nature. If they have sensation and movement, they are animal. Let us examine these: **On minerals** — Mineral bodies are those generated within the earth, blended and mixed together over time in various proportions of quantity and quality. They are of two kinds: strongly composed and weakly composed. The strongly composed, if malleable, include gold, silver, copper, iron, lead, and Chinese iron (tin). If not malleable, they are extremely hard, like ruby and other gemstones. Other bodies — sulfur, bitumen — are generated from mixtures of elements in varying quantities and qualities. Semi-transparent bodies, like collyrium (kohl), are mixed with earthy components. Some are generated from mixtures of sulfur with fine earthy substances, and sulfur itself comes from earthy and airy elements. They are generated when heat acts upon them and purifies them, so that solid transparent bodies form from pure, clear waters. When these accumulate in the earth and the heat of the mine concentrates them, solid dense bodies form. Bodies generated from water and clay form when rain water falls and sunlight acts upon them. Bodies formed from the mixing of different waters with earthy substances, with penetration and blending within the earth, form stony materials. When the heat of the earth acts on them and organizes their composition, the heat of the mine refines them. And thus what the mountains contain — of earth mixed with stone — is described.

On the Properties of Metals and Minerals

It is known that mercury, silver, iron, and lead are produced only within mountains and rocks where the earth is mixed and combined. Sulfur is produced only in damp, soft, and moist earth. Salt is produced only in saline land. Vitriol is produced only in earths that are rotten and decomposed. Among these categories there are many individual varieties of minerals. The foremost of metals, and indeed the first among them, is gold. As they say, metals are formed from refined sulfur and mercury combined together in appropriate measure. The red sulfur provides the color, and it flows through the veins of the earth and heats them; its heat is sustained over a long period underground, so that it does not escape upward or downward. From it arise vapors that are produced, and if the mercury and sulfur are pure but the sulfur lacks sufficient strength, the process is completed before the proper stage of maturation, and thus different varieties of mercury and sulfur give rise to differences in quantity and quality and their associated properties — and this is proven by what the masters of this craft have said. Gold is the noblest of metals: it is not burned by fire, nor is it corrupted by putrefaction, and its temperament is balanced so that neither heat nor cold affects it; it endures fire for a long time without losing quality, and its smell and taste are pleasant, and it is fine and pure. It is one of the greatest blessings of the Almighty, and the ordering of religion and worldly life depends upon it. The manner of the generation of gold has been described. Its nobility lies in this: it is like a guide to all other things — food, clothing, shelter, and so on. Sometimes a person possesses it before he needs it, as if storing it for need; just as when someone's garment wears out and the garment's owner has no more, gold enables him to buy a new one. But the one who is at a middle station — serving both rich and poor — the Almighty has made gold and silver and coin available so that through them one may buy whatever one wishes and sell whatever one wishes. It is for this very reason that the Almighty has condemned hoarding, as He said: 'Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend them in the way of God — give them tidings of a painful punishment.' Whoever hoards gold and buries it — Aristotle has said that gold gives strength to the body when consumed medicinally. If it is made into thin leaves and used, it brightens the eyes and sharpens the sight. Some writers say: if gold is placed in four roads [i.e., at crossroads, as a medicinal trial] and then consumed — as has been described regarding silver: silver likewise, when placed in fire, is burned and when much heat is applied to it, it too becomes purified and refined. The difference between gold and silver and lead is this: if gold encounters sulfurous vapors it becomes tarnished, and if sulfur fumes reach silver it turns black, and its chief property is that it is a purgative and beneficial. Among the Arabs and Hebrews, silver was used as a laxative, and alchemists use it as a coating, and it is beneficial for eye ailments. The nearest to it is tin. The difference between silver, tin, and lead is that silver has more heat from sulfur, while tin and lead are distinguished by the coarseness of their material. Every metal that is given more sulfur than what is appropriate becomes white, and with less it becomes deficient. When acids reach it, it becomes bright and shining, and if needles are made from it...

On the Properties of Iron and Its Virtues
[Page 130]

Water of India and its mines: it is commonly used as a remedy, and is never without benefit. It expels diseases such as cancer and cures ailments of the spleen, liver, and digestion, especially those involving acidity and sharpness. Daily use, even a little, acts like a beneficial substance, and when properly produced, it is like other metals in its qualities. It is exceedingly firm and hard, and beyond the penetrating benefits it provides, it surpasses other metals in many ways. Among its types: Aristotle says that if a piece of iron is bound to someone who lacks courage, his fear will leave him and he will become brave and bold. It brings pleasant dreams and drives away nightmares and sleepiness. If iron filings are used instead of kohl for the eyes, they repel mange and skin diseases. Iron driven away by rust, if placed in the eyes, is beneficial. If iron is polished clean, its shine is like a mirror, and the rust of iron when refined in the mines is beneficial in many ways.

Regarding lead: it is produced and, like iron, has properties mentioned by the learned. Aristotle says that if a diamond is struck on lead with a hammer on an anvil, it will break apart; and if lead is placed against certain creatures, it suppresses their passions and desires. Zinc is produced similarly to lead in its physical nature and is dark in color. From it are made clamps for dogs, and when something is placed in it, it becomes difficult to remove. If a mirror is made from it and one looks into it in a darkened room, the viewer's mind may be affected. If tweezers are made from it and used to pluck hairs, the hair will not grow back.

On the Second Type: Concerning Stones. These substances are produced from the earth by the heat of minerals, and some say they are formed by the influence of lightning and the rays of the planets: Saturn gives them blackness, Jupiter gives them moisture, Mars gives them yellowness, the Sun gives them radiance, Venus gives them perfume, and Mercury gives them their particular qualities. As for the second division: some are produced from water and clay, like when water accumulates in a place, and the heat of the sun concentrates it, and like resin from a tree it hardens and congeals. The differences in stones arise from the differences in their locations, and their treatments include various minerals, borax, sulfur, and other such things.

On Metals and Minerals

If such conditions arise, various types of vitriol (alum/zaj) are produced. If fatty clay does not form, absolute sediment is produced, and in some places there is a water of oxymel (sikanjabīn). This property belongs to that place — just as when the property of air and water becomes like a thorn, it may also be due to the property of the earth, so that it becomes like oxymel. In some places, when creatures like oxymel form, it shows that in this manner it proceeds, or by the exalted [divine will]. When God is angered at someone, He places this property in the earth, and what is produced, because in the essence of the worm there is a group, and the blood from the oxymel of [those creatures] causes harm. They are made to do harm. In between [places] safe from that, both found there and in passing — the fire-striking stone is thus formed. In that place of sustenance (ma'dan) there are many people who have been destroyed, and some have, with divine grace, been able to extract [the mineral], and some of these are recorded in this book in alphabetical order.

Aristotle says: The universal eye-treatment (kuḥl al-kullī) strengthens the eyesight and nerves, prevents [harm], as written in the books. The beauty is apparent, black as if similar in resemblance; it is beneficial and of great use. And if mixed with gold, it is beneficial for [the relevant] body part. As mentioned — may God's blessings be upon him — he said: 'Use it,' for in it is a benefit. It is good for the eyesight and vision. It is used ground up and applied to the eyes for those who seek good sight, and it prevents harm to the eyes. Some people keep it on themselves and the people become beloved friends; it brings fortune of various kinds. Another type has white spots on it; when ground and applied to the eyes of those who suffer from inflamed eyes, it helps. It is like the ash of lead (rasas), applied to the eyes once. When applied, like the juice of pepper, it repels the sting of scorpion at the time it burns; its scent is like Egypt's (musk), so beware of applying it to the neck. Aristotle says that if lead is applied to the eyes, the eyes will water. A little of it applied — the Almighty — it repels harm to the house in the area of the eyes.

Ithmiid [litharge] of gold (Qlimiyā-yi dhahab): It is like red-gold in color; it brings great benefit and gives a golden color. They call it Qlimiyā. If applied to the eyes along with crying and lamentation, it purifies and whitens. If the eyes water, Qlimiyā applied to the eyes at the time of the descent [of the ailment] is beneficial. Qlimiyā of silver (Qlimiyā-yi fizza): Aristotle says about the silver Qlimiyā that it is like gold Qlimiyā but is more beneficial. When applied to corrupt wounds together with arsenic (zirnikh), it is curative and purifying. Its special property is that if a human looks at it, it causes the face to become luminous and brilliant. It may be white or red in color.

If placed in the eye in place of collyrium, it improves the vision. If blood flows from a vein, and healthy [treatment] is needed, it may be used to stop it. If someone suffering from epilepsy uses it, it is beneficial for them, as Aristotle says. If used in decoction form, it makes utensils beautiful and of great benefit to health. If placed opposite the sun during the daytime and [kept] near it, a black shadow will form. It is a type that if bound upon someone, it causes them to become calm. A part of it is from the earth — it is like rock salt (sang-i namak), except that some of it comes forth dissolved in flowing water, and some of it is found in various valleys and mountains and is used as a medicine. Leaf-form (waraq) of it: when made into leaves of gold, mixed with arsenic and purified, it is beneficial. If gold leaf is beaten with arsenic and polished, it becomes pure and good, and the leaf is good for the moisture of trees and for the eyes when applied.

The Third Chapter: On Mineral Substances and Mines, and Their Properties

The judgment is as follows: the fine earth lying in the belly of the ground, in the regions of warm lands, becomes refined, because the earth's interior heat in summer turns cool, since coldness in summer resides in the depths, and [the substance] rests within. If it is moist and oily, then by the mediation of heat it melts, and by the mediation of cold it solidifies and hardens, and in some places bitumen, pitch, and naphtha arise, which are connected to [the nature of the mineral]. The production [of minerals] depends on the combination of qualities — namely heat, cold, moisture, and dryness — for if the moist vapors in the earth's interior become putrid, and heat refines them, rendering them subtle, musk-like and pure, and cold compresses them, then gold and quicksilver are produced. If sulfur mixed with them undergoes intense heat and refinement, and other parts join with it, a clay-like mass forms, which dries, and [minerals like] orpiment and cinnabar are produced. Aristotle said that water and oil, when the constitution is adjusted and each time a certain portion is added, [the compound] settles; and if the earth is thirsty and absorbs it well, and no smoke from the earth rises, then the humors [of the substance] — its smell, taste, color, and form — are kept well. It is said that mercury, when processed, hardens in the earth and becomes firm. If its eye [i.e., its surface] is treated, it blinds [the observer], but its natural constitution, according to the sages, remains for thousands of years. And if one seeks it [i.e., the treatment], as was said, it [the mineral] is composed of earthly, watery, and airy parts and thus [substances like] camphor are born. Some [of these substances] become strong — like an oil produced by coldness — or like the various kinds of sulfur. Among these, the purest red one is [refined] like saffron-gold in quality. Likewise, the one that is red is ranked almost like the nightlight in esteem, and it is very common, but the people who truly understand it and benefit from it are rare.

On the Description of Trees and Their Foliage

Food that gives another strength — the one who depicts it, and expends it, and employs it in this wondrous way, its forms are manifold and varied, bewildering the mind that encounters it, and its opening is thus. The Nourisher, the Most High, the Depicor, formed the kernel and the pit in which the tree and the fruit live, and how remarkable are the forms! Food such as hazelnut, walnut, and pistachio — such foods were sent, and stored like treasures and gifts, some foods being set aside for later, extracted from the fruits, like the best provisions for a journey. Some say: certain foods nourish and are stored as if locked within, and others said: the food takes on the hue of its vessel.

Trees are of two kinds: the first are those that have a trunk — these are called trees (shajar) — and those that have no trunk are called plants (nabat). Large trees are like large animals, and small trees like small animals. Trees whose fruits are not very large, such as the plane tree (dulb) and the teak (saj), their food goes mostly to their trunk, while the food of fruit-bearing trees goes to their fruits — just as among animals: the food of males goes mostly to the body, and of females to the young. An example among insects is the ant, where the food is shared: the food that is young here goes into the growing body, otherwise it would go elsewhere. Thus the branches, veins, arteries, and bark of trees are like the veins and sinews of a living body. A plant whose leaves are like those of small-leaved plants with their sap flowing in the middle, like a river running through it — what a wonder it is! The trees are dressed in leaves as if clothed, like wool and hair and felt — the Creator has dressed them in this way, and has arranged the leaves against the differences of wind and weather. At the top the fresh fruits are set upright, nourished by the moisture of the roots, fresh in the shade of the leaves.

A scholar came and saw it, and they spoke to each other about injustices and cruelties. They left and the man went into the wilderness and returned, and he had told someone to stay. On the Description of the Date Palm (Nakhla) and Its Properties

For two years it yields fruit abundantly, requiring no laborer to harvest it, bringing forth its produce without effort. This tree, which I wish to describe, brings forth fruit a hundredfold. It has been said that the owner of a palm grove, if he tends it year after year, gains great benefit from it; and it is well known that the male and female palms must be planted near one another so that they may receive the pollen from one another, and the male palm's pollen must be brought to the female so that it may be fertilized; if the female palm is separated from the male, it will bear no fruit.

It has been reported that there are two types: one is distinguished and the other is of another kind. It has been mentioned in the chapter on its virtues that each year the harvest comes twice, and the date clusters grow and produce their fruit. The palm tree requires a caretaker, and its growth and cultivation must be attended to properly. It is said that the male and female palms have a natural affinity and attraction for one another, and if one is separated from the other, the fruit diminishes. The owners of palm groves know well that if travelers pass by, they should be generous with their produce.

The Persians are fond of this tree and consider it among the most beneficial and pleasant of trees. It has been said that drinking its sap boiled is beneficial, and its various parts are used in different preparations and medicines.

Naturalists have described it thus: some call it the "four-footed" (chahāri) and some call it the "parrot-colored" (bāzī rang). Some say it is a collective name. Those who study the wonders of creation say that it drives away harmful creatures from the dwelling. Its tongue, when dried and worn as an amulet, is said to protect against envy and the evil eye.

The scholars of wonders have noted: if its stomach contents are examined, various remarkable things are found. Its ashes mixed with oil make a substance that treats certain ailments. The passage discusses four types of mental and physical faculties, their benefits, and how they relate to human well-being and conduct. The text is structured as follows:

It begins by stating that if a young man is overcome by certain appetites and desires, the capacity for reason may diminish. The pursuit of pleasure weakens memory, causes forgetfulness, and undermines proper conduct. This is described as the first category of faculty, namely the appetitive power (quwwat shahwaniyya).

The second faculty is the irascible power (quwwat ghadabiyya), which drives a young man toward boldness and confrontation. This faculty, if not properly balanced, leads one toward beastly behavior, since it operates without the guidance of wisdom and proper nourishment.

The fourth type — the rational faculty in its most complete form — is then discussed. The first level of this faculty is that which disposes a person to seek fine and praiseworthy things through intellectual virtue. The second level enables one to benefit from theoretical knowledge and rational discourse. The third level leads one to the acquisition of sciences and the perfection of crafts, through which sciences and industries are learned and practical action is undertaken.

The text then cites a saying attributed to the Commander of the Faithful (Imam Ali), to the effect that reason is what enables a person to hear, obey, and benefit from guidance, while the one who lacks reason is like an animal in human form.

The narrative then shifts to an anecdote set in the context of a physician and a patient. A physician is called to examine a sick person. A companion who was present marvels at this, and the physician explains: 'If a person is alive, the body reveals what was consumed; if dead, the signs remain nonetheless.' The passage ends with this observation about the diagnostic power of careful medical attention.

**Chapter on the Religions of the Romans (al-Rum):**

The Romans were a people who prized reason and philosophy, and among their kings there were those who ruled with justice and sought the welfare of their subjects. They were fond of learning and debate, and their scholars considered it essential to educate the youth in noble character and sound morals, so as to guard them against arrogance and pride. 

One of their kings asked a learned physician about a certain ailment, and was told to go to Syria where the people of that faith (Nestorian Christians) could be found. He went to Syria and embraced the Christian faith, bringing all those around him back to Rome, and thereafter invited his people to convert. They accepted his call and became Christians.

Men such as Sarpius, Qaddus al-Hads, and others were among those who spread the faith and came to the monastery. It is said that thereafter the faith was divided into three sects and many groups, each with its own practices — on feast days they would gather for music, merriment, eating, and celebration.

On the Page of Poetic Meters

Section on Meters (al-Awzān) and their Types:

Those were in the meter of Ḍarb, and we will mention the meters and their forms — Section on Meters (al-Awzān).

The Ṭawīl and its principles: it is [built on] mafāʿīlun, four times, and the verse begins — this was reported from antiquity. In the era of Khosrow and Shapour.

The Basīṭ: its principle is fāʿilatun qāʿim ʿaraj four times, and the verse begins — that people [use it] mixed.

The Wāfir: its principle is mustafʿin fāʿilun four times, and the verse begins — this is the ruling upon it.

The Muḍāriʿ: its foundation is mafāʿilun six times, and the verse begins — as kings [employ it] for their exaltation.

The Kāmil: its principle is mutafāʿilun, repeated in verses — [as in the example] 'The time passed and the days went by.'

The Rajaz: its principle is mustafʿilun, repeated in verses — 'the pasture-lands, their names, their lengths, their customs.'

The Rasm and its principle, and the verse — 'It has been long since the pilgrimage and the journey of al-Shaṭārī.'

Again the verse begins — 'May the Khāqān, when he departs, not cease to dwell in the encampment of relief.'

The Khurūj: its principle, again verse — 'My caller calls, and my summoner summons; the goal is reached, the longing fulfilled.'

Abu Zayd said: 'I remain always awaiting relief from Egypt.'

The Muqtaḍab: its principle — 'The most courtly of them in temperament, fairest of face, sweetest of expression.'

The Munsariḥ: its principle — 'The finest of them in conduct, most gracious in virtue, noblest in character.'

The Maqṭūʿ: eight times in verse — 'May the guardian of speech, the orderer of eloquence, have peace.'

The Circles (Dāʾiras): The two circles of Ṭawīl and Basīṭ and the Madbūr are a discussion: they contain different meters, and are called [by scholars] of metrical theory and compound meters, of the particular and auditory, and the Ṭawīl. They are considered [as sharing] a single structural pillar (watad) from which the first [is derived], and established, and from it the second removes a foot — hence 'Muʾakhkhar' — and the Sabab, and the proximate watad, and the Sabab separates from it, [and so] in Fawlun and Basīṭ it breaks down.

As for the Muṭawwal, the precedent [element] and the Mudabbar are Basīṭ and Wāfir, and the Kāmil circle exists — thus the author says: here another [meter], of sevenfold repetition, its components and its members are made precedent, since the first has been established as stronger. Distinct.

The separator (fāṣila): when you wish to shorten the Kāmil, remove ʿalun — taking it from mafāʿil — and [similarly for] the Wāfir. This is known.

And if they are compounded — since the Rājaz is thus, the sevenfold being made precedent — they do not break, since they are placed as precedent.

When you wish to derive [one meter] from another — as the Mukhīl [removes] lun — you must do so, and similarly the Muqtaḍab.

These names were given among the Persians, as the author mentions, and this circle [is called] al-Muṣarrāʿ — remove the first Mustafʿilun and [keep] the second ʿalun — thus you transform it. And if you wish to produce the Muḍāriʿ from the Sarīʿ, remove the second ʿalun, and thus you transform it.

And if you wish to derive the Munsariḥ from the Sarīʿ as a shortened form, remove the first Mafāʿīlātun — thus you transform it. And by this method of shortening, whenever you wish the Muqtaḍab, [proceed] thus.

And this circle — know its parts — is called 'the Muʿāqab Circle' because its components interact, and their characteristic is that they intermingle; and the author has brought them together and set them down, and their derivation from each other without the dissolution of the form is not broken.

The verse goes: 'Our evening and our morning — our glory, our wealth, our bounty — our era is the most noble among people.'

The verse of the first [foot]: when in its parts it becomes light — the second being the Muḍārakata — and the Alif which is in the parts [makes it complete].

Concerning the Story of the Accursed Satan

The inhabitants would perish and be destroyed in the land. A great army came, and those people were captured. Azazil (Iblis) was there from among the jinn, and he grew up there. It is said in the Quran: 'He was of the jinn' (Surah Al-Kahf). The chiefs of his followers whose names are Shar, Aflum, Dasim, Zawbar, and others — each one is assigned to a particular kind of evil: the lord of fornication tempts people's eyes toward it; another causes lying; another brings enmity between people.

Chapter: On the Stratagems of Satan Among the Children of Israel

There was a man called Barsisa among the Children of Israel. He was a worshipper, and Satan wanted to test him. Satan sent him a girl, claiming she was a patient who needed care. Barsisa took her in to treat her. Satan kept whispering to him until he was led astray and committed a great sin with her, and she became pregnant. Satan then whispered to him that he should kill her to conceal the matter, and he did so and buried her. Then Satan went to her family and revealed to them what Barsisa had done to their daughter. They seized him and brought him before the authorities for judgment. As Barsisa was being led to execution, Satan came to him and said: 'I am the one who brought you to this situation — if you wish, I can save you. Prostrate yourself before me.' Barsisa prostrated before Satan, and at that moment Satan abandoned him, saying to the people: 'I am free of this man.' Thus the story ended with Barsisa's destruction, and this is the meaning of God's words: 'Like Satan when he says to man, disbelieve, and when he disbelieves, says: I am free of you.'

The companions then gathered and built a place of worship and devoted themselves to worship. Satan went to one of them, came to him, and whispered to him, and named himself as a holy guide. This led to great harm in their religion. Eventually one of them apostasized, and then the others followed. They cut down a tree nearby.

Satan said: 'Why are you cutting down this tree?' They said: 'We are cutting it for firewood.' Satan said: 'No, do not cut it — this tree is worthy of worship.' The worshipper said: 'My worship is silence...' and then Satan [continued his trickery].

Chapter on the Mention of Some Demons and Jinn: It is said that the wisest and most clever of demons desire to mislead people. They say that among the demons are those called Ghuls, and they take on terrible forms to frighten people. Ali ibn Abi Talib described their nature, saying: 'I have seen the Ghul — from its head to its navel it resembles a human, and from the navel downward its legs are like a donkey's, and some companions reported seeing a Ghul on a journey.' It is said in various accounts that the Ghul appears mostly in the form of women and in deserts, and if one recites certain verses over it, it will play games. Whoever sees a beautiful form on the road, let him beware — they appear beautiful but are actually demons who drive people mad. The daughters of Zulab (a type of female demon) wander about in Egypt's outskirts, and if one approaches them, they take the form of a human and cause great destruction to the people.

On the Description of Animals and Their Properties

It has been heard that some of these birds are used as remedies for certain ailments, and their properties have been noted. Among these, some are used mixed with the droppings of certain insects, and their use is described in connection with various beneficial treatments. When the feathers of certain birds are ground and applied, they produce beneficial effects on the skin and hair, and the blessed fowl is described as attracting good fortune.

It is said that the partridge (Durrāj) utters certain calls and songs from the north, and its sounds carry particular properties depending on the direction of the wind — from south or north — and one type of it can imitate the call of the francolin (Durrāj) from a great distance, driving away enemies, and if it is caught and kept, it brings blessings.

Regarding the rooster (Khurūs): Its crowing at dawn signals the time of departure, and it is said that it brings stability and drives away evil. According to tradition, God says: 'When the rooster crows, it is because it has seen an angel.' It is therefore like a guardian that keeps the devil away from the house. Its fat is also said to have medicinal properties.

It is said that the rooster belongs to the category of noble birds, and keeping it in the house drives away the devil. Among its special properties: if its blood is taken and applied in certain ways, it brings benefits. If its meat is cooked and consumed with certain preparations, it strengthens the body. The domestic hen (Murgh-i khāki) is also remarkable — when it crows at dawn like a rooster, something extraordinary occurs in the morning.

On the Page of Animals: Concerning the Porcupine

Another [account]: it repels harmful creatures and snakes; if a mouse encounters it, it is killed. Its presence in a house keeps away harm, and if one binds [something] with its quills, the cure comes easily. If a woman takes [its parts] and uses them...

They say that moths are attracted to fire and burn in it, and one must take note of this. Avicenna (Sheikh al-Ra'is) says that its warmth is beneficial, and in cold weather it provides protection. Some say that if seven of them are placed together for a certain number of days, they bring about a certain benefit. It is said that from a human body a sweat is produced, and its flesh resembles dog meat. If its fat is mixed with black oil and applied to the feet, it is beneficial; and if one rubs it on the body, it provides strength.

If a woman rubs herself with its blood and looks at a man, that man will be overcome with love. If thirty [porcupines] are killed and their flesh rendered, and one is rubbed with it, one will be safe. Some say that if its quills are put into a tree and fire is brought near, the tree will die. Its quills, when shot, strike like arrows, and the animal can shoot them. When threatened, it rolls into a ball and its quills stand on end so that no predator can approach it.

Its young are born like other animals. It is said that the porcupine is larger than a hedgehog and quieter. Its meat, when cooked, has medicinal properties. If its fat is boiled and poured into the ear, it cures earache. Rubbing it on the body treats skin conditions.

Its bile, when swallowed, is harmful, but its meat, when cooked with vinegar and eaten, benefits those with bladder and urinary problems. If a rabid dog bites someone and the porcupine's flesh is applied to the wound, it draws out the poison. Its meat, prepared and eaten regularly, benefits many ailments.

In sum, the porcupine is an animal of subtle and beneficial qualities, known to scholars for its many virtues. It is sought after everywhere and is prized among animals. It has both faults and merits; the merits outweigh the faults. If its faults are revealed, they too have their use, and if its virtues are described, they are even greater.

On the Description of Wild Animals and Livestock
Chapter

The pure, swift, and well-structured [creatures] — as the scholars have noted — are among those which God has brought forth and placed [in creation], such that whatever befalls them of hardship is quickly resolved and passes away. The foundation of their correction is firmness, and the causes of their disorder are to be managed carefully, so that their temperament remains balanced. In the best seasons and finest circumstances, through the diversity of their nourishment and various moistures, they are sustained. In their dwellings they construct [shelters], and upon the fine, gentle trees they make their homes and lay up provisions from the scents and aromas of trees, taking fine, subtle nourishment.

Among their most remarkable qualities is that they store provisions for themselves from within themselves, and from the finest and most delicate things, so that the stored substance becomes thick and condensed; this food is self-generated from within. They lay up reserves for themselves and store away supplies, and some of their dwellings serve as storehouses throughout summer and winter. From these reserves they provision themselves for winter, when they go out from their homes and are struck by cold, rain, and harsh wind. Then when spring comes, if food is found outside, they venture forth; and they construct remarkable structures. When smoke is blown at them, they flee and scatter, and from wherever honey is sought, other honey comes, and one part goes elsewhere.

Honey produced in the tender, fine [comb] is from new [comb], yellow honey is from old [comb], and red honey is as fragrant as ambergris — this is from the finest places. Its benefit for those of hot temperament is well established, for it is cooling in constitution. From it, sekmenjin [a preparation] is made, and from it cold remedies are derived, and whatever is fit for [medical] use — its wax is taken and used as a remedy. As for the dwelling walls of the palm-tree hive, the wax comes from the hive-combs, and the beeswax and gum are from there, and the honey comes from the bees.

Bees are among the most greedy of creatures for their hive: their dwelling is like a house with chambers and rooms and stories, and the water does not reach the stored provisions, and some of their chambers are specially set apart so that water does not reach them. When the bee is stung by [another creature], as soon as it smells something, the most [senior] bees detect the scent and come to drive others away, warning them not to approach; and if a small bee is gripped and squeezed by them, they release venom and it dies, and when its husk is shed, the colony senses that the time has come for [a new] owner, and the others follow. If they do not [swarm properly], they separate into groups, and if their house is disturbed they scatter.

Among [the species], there is a kind of fly called nawfas — a type of bee finer than ordinary flies, and it belongs to a double-winged [variety]. It has a long tail and is small in body, and when it is provoked and squeezed, the flesh on which it [alights] causes festering, and if its skin is burned, the ashes applied as an ointment to joints [provide benefit], and if the compound of its [secretion] is used to rub [an area], it clears away dark spots like gold.

The account of Imam Reza (peace be upon him) who requested that so many things be brought before him in their proper form and with their instruments. So the devil appeared before this gathering in the form of a being resembling a monkey, with a strange face and odd features: it had four arms, two on each side, and its feet were peculiar in shape, its body was bound and tied behind it and painted in strange colors of blue and dark hues, and it wore a cap on its head, and it was an ugly and bizarre creature. It said to the people gathered near: 'I have come here to show you the pleasures of music and instruments — the flute, the drum, the lute — just as the sound of the crow enchants the ear. I occupy people with my own voice and power.' Then it was told: 'You capture the hearts of the righteous with your allure and draw them away from obedience to God.' It said: 'I guard myself among the righteous, and with this trap I capture their hearts with my scent, and when they are not mindful of God I lead them toward women and desires, drawing them away, and these are the ways of Satan, who leads people to obey him and to turn their hands away from obedience to God. May the curse of God be upon him and upon all of this.'
